BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: That the quorum of the Select Standing Committee on Banking and Commerce be reduced from 21 to 11 members.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: At the last meeting of the Banking and Commerce Committee, a resolution was passed asking this House to authorize a reduction in the number of the quorum. It was then urged by a member of the House who is also a member of the committee that, perhaps, the discussion which took place at that time would lead to a larger attendance at the meeting of this and other committees. The Banking and Commerce Committee was called for business for last Friday morning at 11 o'clock. We had no quorum. The committee was called again for this morning at 11 o'clock, and, although there was present a solicitor interested in one of the Bills to he up for discussion, and though that solicitor endeavoured to drum up a quorum, he failed to do so. I understand that the new Banking Act will be referred to the Banking and Commerce Committee this session. If so, there will be a large number of meeting's of the committee, and I think it is very important that (business be not impeded, and, with that view, that the quorum be reduced, to a possible number. It has been urged, as the members of the committee number 132, that 21 is not an unreasonably large quorum. But I would point out to you, Mr. 'Speaker, and to the House, that while there are 221 members of this House, 20 constitute a quorum. It does not seem unreasonable that we should have the same proportionate quorum on committees of the House.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: When the committee proposed the reduction of the quorum, their recommendation was that it should be reduced from 21 to 15. The chairman (Mr. Miller) now proposes that it should be reduced to 11. I think that number is low, and especially in view of the very important Bill likely to come 'before the committee, the general banking Bill. I think that the quorum of the committee to consider so important a Bill should be more than 11 members. It seems to me that 15 would he a reasonable number, but quite low enough.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext:
I do not think that the House should make -any change in the quorum of the Banking and 'Commerce Committee. My hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) spoke of the meeting this morning. Well, this morning, three different committees were called for the same hour-eleven	o'clock ; Public
Accounts, Agriculture and Banking and Commerce. If the chairman of committees are not more careful in seeing to it that committees are not called for the same hour and day, they cannot expect members to attend in such numbers as, I am sure, my hon. friend from South Grey would expect in the case of a committee that has to deal with such important questions as those which come before the Bank-

ing and Commerce Committee. I rather think that, when any change is made with respect to the quorum of these committees, it should be by a change in the rules of the House, and not by selecting one committee for change while leaving the others as they are. This is a matter that ought to receive very careful consideration by the House, and should not be done in this sudden way of simply passing a resolution. Perhaps it would have been all right to pass a resolution of this kind even with respect to the Banking and Commerce Committee at some other time, but my hon. friend knows that there is to come	before this committee the
most important matter that will come before	any committee this session,
the change in the banking law. 1 think that the committee should not take up the consideration of these very important enactments without at least 21 members out of the 221 members of this House present. I suggest to the chairman that he leave this over for further consideration and for more thorough discussion in the Banking and Commerce Committee itself. Surely he will not wish to press a matter of this kind now. I think that when the discussion was on in the House the other day the general expression of opinion was in apposition to the proposal to reduce the quorum of this committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.

speechtext:
I rise with some diffidence to discuss this matter as I am not a member of the Banking and Commerce Committee, but I desire to be heard because this is a very important time in connection with the work of this committee and it is a very important committee, and its action affects the interest of all classes of people in Canada. It seems to me that the difficulty pointed out by the chairman of the committee (Mr. Miller) is not overcome by his motion. Did I understand him to say that when the committee was 114
called to meet a few days ago no one attended?

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: I understood him to say that no one was present. And how many were present at the meeting called for this morning?

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: That, I presume, was after the drumming up referred to by the chairman. This difficulty arises out of a general condition of things, and not out of anything connected with this committee specially. I have taken the liberty more than once of calling the attention ot the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to thi3 subject, No matter how good and active a member of parliament a man may be, he cannot be in two places at the same time. Nor can the member of parliament do his work properly by trying to divide his attention between two committees that are meeting at the same time. The trouble arises through summoning a number of committees for the same day. And The reason for that-which may be regarded as another difficulty-is that we do not summon committee meetings for Monday or Friday.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: Yes, the Public Accounts.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: -I am corrected as to the Public Accounts Committee. I venture again to suggest to the Prime Minister that it would be better if we had committees meeting on Mondays and Fridays as a regular thing. There is no reason why members should be encouraged to absent themselves from attendance on their public duties on these days. If the suggestions I make were adopted, and if the membership of each committee were reduced to a reasonable number, the difficulty we are now discussing could not arise. Now, the special reason why I speak at this time is that a most important matter is supposed to come before the Banking and Commerce Committee this session. I have heard the rumour that the government does not intend to introduce and pass the Banking Act this session. I trust that is only an idle rumour.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: It has been introduced.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: I said ' introduce and pass.' I have heard, since the Bill was introduced, that the government does not intended to move forward and pass it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: No foundation for that.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: I am glad to hear from the Finance Minister that there is no foundation for that. I would urge the Finance Minister to get a little active in regard to this matter, and not leave it till the last of the session, when, as we know by experience, matters that come up do not receive very close attention. The Banking and Commerce Committee this session has more important work before it than any other committee of the House, I venture to say; and I can promise my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) who moved this motion that when the Banking Act comes up for consideration there will be no lack of members there, and there will be no lack of spectators either. The country is -aroused on the question of the banking law of Canada, not only by reason of the Farmers' Bank, but by reason of other earlier events, and of events that have supervened. When this Bill comes up to 'be dealt with, we want a full (attendance of members, we want a quorum which will guarantee responsibility to the people, and we want a condition of things which will insure a most careful and rigid handling of that question. Therefore, speaking with a sense of responsibility, I for one decidedly object to a change in the number constituting the quorum of the Banking and Commerce Committee.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: I do not agree with the remarks of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Lennox) as to the work being less efficiently done by a smaller quorum of members. I think 11 or 15 members of that committee are able to do the work just as well as twenty-one. As a matter of fact, referring to one very important matter, the Lumsden affair, the House felt perfectly safe, and in the opinion of my hon. friend the interests of the country were perfectly safe, in the hands of only seven members.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: The four did better than the seven.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, after some of them saw fit to leave the committee, the affairs of the country were thoroughly well managed by four members of this House who were on that committee. Now it occurs to me at the moment that there are two ways of bringing the 130 members of that committee to a sense of their duty, to bring them into action. The first way is by persuasion, by sweet remembrance of the duty of each one of them. The second way is by chastisement-my English expression may be poor

speechtext:
It is all right.
Mr. WILSON (Laval) but if it is all right so much the better. I was a victim of the second way a few days ago. In the Montreal ' Gazette ' and Montreal * Star ' a Mr. FIELDING.
list was published of the members who were absent when the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) presented his motion asking for delay in regard to the reciprocity arrangement; and the insinuation was made in those papers that the member for Laval was not in the House for the very good reason that he approved of the motion of the member for Jacques Cartier. Now, I would propose that the members of the Banking and Commerce Committee should be_ chastised in the same way in order to induce them to do their duty, and that the names of the absent ones should be published. But when the names of the absent are published, I for one will be under a great disadvantage, because the names are usually published in alphabetical order, and as my name begins with the letter W, it comes last on the list-always excepting one other hon. member of this House, that is the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright). He may be the wrong Mr. Wright some times, or he may be the right Mr. Wright at other times. So I think perhaps the best way to settle the matter would be for each member of this committee to perform his duty. Now the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) used an expression about members getting ' busy.' Well, perhaps I am not entitled to speak for other members in this regard, but there is another member of this House, a very prominent one, who is nearly always busy at his duty somewhere else than in the committee. I venture to suggest to my hon. friend from Simcoe that he urge upon his friend, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), to attend more often the Banking and Commerce Committee, where his services would be so valuable.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext:
I think hon. members lose sight of the fact that we do not want to change the number of members on that committee. Everybody can attend the committee, and it is their duty to do so, even if the quorum is reduced. I quite agree in the view of the importance of the Bank Bill that is to come before the committee. I might also mention the Insurance Bill which was before the committee, when it was very difficult to get a quorum, although the Bill was just as important perhaps as the Banking Bill which is to come before the committee. In the case of the Insurance Bill it iwas very difficult indeed to get a quorum, and nearly every morning the chairman had to preside over the committee when there was not a quorum present. I do not see any' reason why the quorum of the committee should not be reduced, because at present we do not get a full quorum there. It is not fair

to those who do attend to keep them waiting from 15 to 20 minutes or half an hour for other members to turn up. So far as I am concerned, I strongly endorse the recommendation to change the quorum so that we can get on with the business.

maintopic: BANKING AND COMMERCE COMMITTEE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF QUORUM.
speechtext:
This is a matter not of much interest to any except those members who are interested in the work of the committee. They have been doing business morning after morning without any quorum at all, and we thought that it would be better to do business with a quorum that could be obtained under the authority of the House. The members of the committee who are in favour of reducing the quorum are those who are regularly present. I do not care to press the matter contrary to the wishes of the House, and if it is the wish of the House that the quorum should not be reduced, I beg to withdraw the motion.
Motion withdrawn.

Before the orders of the day are called I desire to ask a question of the government. On the front page of the Montreal ' Gazette ' of this morning, I find the following:
Washington, D.C., February 14.-* We are preparing to annex Canada,' announced Champ Clark, leader of the Democratic party in the House of Representatives, in the course of the discussion on the proposed reciprocity treaty. Immediately after he had made that sensational statement, he and all the other Democrats except three from Louisiana, proceeded to vote for the passage [DOT]** reciprocity agreement.

As a result of Democratic support of the proposed treaty, the fiual vote by which it was passed in the House to-night showed 220 members to be for it and 92 against it. Eighty-nine representatives refused their support to a measure backed by a Republican president. On the other hand, with the exception of the three votes mentioned, all the Democrats supported the titular leader of the opposition party, a thing that has not happened in this country for many years.
Annexation of Canada was the keynote of the speech by Mr. Clark, who will be Speaker of the next house, in whipping the members of his party into line in support of the reciprocity agreement with Canada. Not once, nor twice, but thrice, did he boldly declare:
' We are preparing to annex Canada/
Further down it says:
Mr. Clark, who at a public meeting yesterday joined with President Taft in advocating reciprocity between the United States and the whole world, has now called attention to the rumored movement of the ' one flag, the Stars and Stripes, from Central America to the north pole.'
Has the attention of the government been drawn to this matter? Have the government taken any cognizance of this statement, and if so what is their intention? Do they propose immediately withdrawing the reciprocity agreement if the foregoing report is verified.

speechtext: ["The hour of adjournment is so near, that I cannot continue this discussion longer. I have heard no substantial reason advanced against this proposal, which will bear investigation. Every interest of Canada, is guarded. It gives us three markets, instead of two. Every interest of Great Britain is guarded. If a day comes when Great Britain is able to enter into better arrangements with the colonies and to bring us all together, our hands are free. If we become a greater and more prosperous people, if we become a richer people, we shall be all the stronger as a British nation and a part of the British Empire, and we shall never, with my consent, be other than a part of the British Empire. But why mix this matter up with questions affecting our political relations? The whole and sole question foT us is, have we made a good bargain? As for me and the part of the country which I represent, this proposal will be welcomed as one of the most progressive acts of a government which for 14 years has shown nothing but progress, development and success in Canada.\nProgress reported.\nAt six o'clock, House adjourned.", 'Thursday, February 16, 1911.']

In the county I have the honour to represent there is a very strong feeling in respect to these matters. Throughout the western part of Ontario, at the pi'esent moment, large sums of money are being subscribed to send delegations to the government to explain the position of specific interests that will be affected if these tariff changes become law. Will the government give serious consideration to the representations of these interests if they are made to the government? I may anticipate by saying that a general answer that the government will listen to all complaints of everybody will not be quite sufficient. I want to know if the government will give serious consideration to these matters, or whether it will be better for these gentlemen to stay at home on the ground that this proposal will not be changed?
To this the Prime Minister replied:
We will give most serious consideration to all the interests represented, reserving our judgment.
I think the Prime Minister will frankly admit that the unanimous views of these men, practical fruit growers, all of them, men who are thoroughly familiar with the multitudinous details of their own special business, presented, the Prime Minister will also admit, in a fair and moderate and absolutely convincing manner, should have been listened to with a great deal of attention. From 1883 to 1899 I lived in that district, devoting myself entirely to fruit growing. I may fairly say that I know the conditions as no other man in the House knows them. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs could not have listened to that careful presentation backed by statistics, and presented not by opponents of this government, but largely by Mr. FIELDING
their political friends and not realize how grave an injustice had been done these great interests. I am not going to repeat those arguments, but two phases of this matter I will touch on for a minute. In that belt of country stretching from the Niagara river to the city of Hamilton, a country, Sir, which is the pride and delight of every Canadian who knows it, there are 1,000,000 peach trees in cultivation, roughly 10,000 acres. A low estimate of their value would be from three to five million dollars. There is absolutely no doubt that this special and vastly important branch of horticultural industry is grievously injured by these proposals. I can tell this House that western New York has been earnestly hoping for some such thing as this. Even with the duty it has been possible for some of the canners to buy at twenty cents a basket, or a cent a pound, on the New York side of the river, the duty protecting the Canadian grower so that he can get a livable price. Let me point out to the Prime Minister another grievous wrong done. Amongst other matter presented on that day was the following memorial:
To the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, in parliament assembled:
We, the undersigned, the president and executive committee of tire Old Country Association, composed entirely of men born and bred in the British Isles, and the great majority of whom are engaged in the fruit industry, respectfully and earnestly beg to draw the attention of the Dominion government to the peculiar hardship which will be imposed upon us should this proposed tariff legislation come into effect.
We have been induced to leave Great Britain, and to come to this peninsula, and to invest our capital in the purchase, planting and general improvement of fruit lands in a large measure owing to the very wide distribution of official pamphlets and other literature emanating from Canada, and distributed throughout the British Isles, positively stating that ' the Ontario grower is protected in the home market by a high tariff against foreign grown fruit and vegetables, and thus enjoys that market without serious competition from outside sources.'
The amount of customs tariffs on the various fruits is specifically stated in these pamphlets and literature; and in order that this particular advantage to the Canadian grower may be clearly understood by the Britisher, this tariff scale is not only set forth in Canadian money but is also set forth in the coinage of Great Britain. Under the bplief that these conditions would be stable, we have not only sunk our own capital, but have been instrumental in bringing many of our countrymen here to invest in this growing industry, which owing to the steady rise of recent vears in the values of land now requires a large amount of capital to purchase and equip even the small farms the majority of us own, and to provide for the maintenance

of our families during the years it takes to bring an orchard into bearing.
(Signed),WILLIAM BRIGGS, President.
"	R.	Y. GRACE,"	H.	LAMPARD,

speechtext:
"	A.	BAKER,"	A.	N. DAVIS,
Executive committee.
St. Catharines, Feb. 4, 1911.
Now, Sir, the facts are as stated. Some of these men, and there are a great number of them, were sent by the Dominion government officials to the officials of the Ontario government, because, as is natural, that government had special knowledge of the Ontario fruit districts. Canada invited them to come and embark their capital. Canada set forth the advantages they would get. Stability of tariff in relation to the fruit industry was assured them. They came, scores of them. They have been a splendid type of immigrant. These men have done what I wish Englishmen would do elsewhere, joined themselves together in an association to'help others who come here in their initial steps; to assist them in learning to know Canada and to so adjust themselves to its conditions as to become worthy citizens of their adopted country. They have invested their thousands, and have in many cases brought their orchards almost to the bearing point. They have found it an expensive process, more especially as they had to nav, and still have to pay under these proposals, heavy duties on their spraying machines, their tools, their implements with which they had to equip themselves. Is it any wonder that this large body of men feel that Canada has betrayed them?	.
Bir, wbat was the character ot the Prime Minister's answer to these 800 Canadian citizens? I do not want to use extravagant language; but no man ean have heard the Prime Minister without feeling that it was a hopelessly trivial, unbusinesslike and disappointing answer that he gave. He made no attempt whatever to give a serious answer to a serious statement. He showed no appreciation of the issues involved. I do not expect that my right ho.u. friend should be intimately acquainted with the details of the fruit industry, but I did expect, and these men had the right to expect, that the First Minister of the . country would at least have given an intelligible and intelligent answer to their presentment. He told them that the Canadian orchards were the finest in the world-that the Montreal melon was eaten in New York. If he attempted any answer at all to arguments, it was this, that some time before a delegation of farmers had come to the government, and that amongst them the fruit interests were voiced in favour of free fruit, and therefore, as the opinion of the growers was a divided opinion, the government found it a difficult matter to deal with. Sir, if the delegation on December 16 from the west had been a delegation of the fruit growers of the Dominion, I could understand such a reply; but what are the facts? One gentleman from Nova Scotia spoke-and I have already dealt with this statement and shown that the Prime Minister cannot shelter himself there. One man from New Brunswick spoke, and I cannot find that he spoke with authority even from that province; but his remarks were to the effect that he would find a better market for his hay and potatoes and turnips in the United States, and would have saved $200 on his strawberry crop by free fruit. Sir, it is almost inconceivable that the Prime Minister of this country could cite such evidence in detail as a reason for refusing these eight hundred men, and the thousands whom they represented, their requests. One man also from Ontario spoke, an apple grower of Norfolk who has had business connections in the United States for some time past and is interested in shipping some of his fruit in that direction. But even from Norfolk much of the fruit has gone to the prairies, where it will now not be able to withstand the free competition from the western states, afld I may point out that even if every Norfolk apple grower wanted free fruit, which is far from being the fact, Norfolk county, excellent district though it may be, is only tenth in the list of the fruit growing counties of Ontario. Its orchard areas are not so valuable as the single strip of peach area to which I have alluded, and not one-tenth of the area of British Columbia, where the damage brought by these proposals is deplorable. Yet, Sir, this was all the argument brought to the consideration of this great delegation's case.
I have read the report of the western farmers' delegation very carefully, xney stated that they had come to Ottawa at great expense and inconvenience, but that they felt justified in incurring it all in order to show the government they were in earnest. Sir, was that still greater delegation on February 10, representing the fruit industry, less in earnest? In the report of the western farmers' delegation 17 pages are taken up in a lengthy plea for government ownership and operation of terminal elevators-this was what they pleaded for at greatest length; 34 pages in a plea for the establishment of the chilled meat industry, 7 pages in urging the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, and

amendments to the Railway Act, 8 pages in dealing with the customs tariff, chiefly, I might almost say solely, with the argument for a lowering of the duties on manufactures and on easier entry into ttie United States' markets for grain and cattle. One of the most forcible addresses on customs tariff matters was from Mr. Thos. McMillan. He said on page 43:
We come before you asking no favours, but we claim that agriculture should under the tariff be placed on an equal footing with the other industrial enterprises of the land.
That applies with equal force to the horticulturists. Let me commend it to the Minister of Customs. But, Sir, in the whole of this report there is but a scant page which deals at all with fruit, and which even then deals with it in the fragmentary and unrepresentative way which I have already touched on. To say that the western farmers were making tne abolition oi the fruit duties an important part ot tneir case is to mistake plain facts. To say that the fruit interests were in any adequate way represented at that time is also entirely contrary to the facts. The Prime Minister may have been in a tight place- he may have already made up his mind; but it would have been fairer to have told these men not to come than to have treated them in so shabby, so unconvincing, so hopelessly inadequate a manner. Man after mdfi, family after family, in that district will see his business prospects clouded, will see his long years of waiting unrewarded; and it leaves but a bitter taste in the mouth to be told in reply that they must go home and sacrifice themselves and their hopes-not, as the Prime Minister suggested, for other horticulturists, but for other and not more important interests, who are being catered to by these proposals.
Now, Sir, I wish to turn for a short time to the case of the fruit growing industry in my own province of British Columbia. In no part of Canada is this national industry hit with equal force by the proposals before the House. Not within the whole range of our economic history in Canada can there be found so strong an instance of a great industry, which has deserved, and has had some encouragement and some aid from all governments, being deprived of such help without the shadow of an equivalent, or of compensation. I can emphatically state that the pressure of the western fruit-growing states, which are already faced with great difficulties in disposing of their large surplus of second grade fruit, is responsible for President Taft's desire to obtain the privilege of free entry into Canadian markets.
The very first fruit trees planted in British soil west of the Rocky mountains were Mr. BURRELL
planted in the life time of many members in this House. Until the eighties the vast interior of the province was practically a terra incognita. Such settlements as there were made under unusual hardships and drawbacks. The trees for the earlier orchards were, in many cases, brought hundreds of miles on horseback over dangerous and difficult mountain trails. Mining and cattle ranching formed the chief activities of the huge, but sparsely settled, country. But there were not wanting evidences of the special suitability of the climate and soil for the production of fruit. The coming of the Canadian Pacific railway stimulated the work, but even up to 1891 but slow progress had been made, and it was not until 1897 that the first shipment of fruit was sent beyond the limits of the province itself. Commercial horticulture in British Columbia practically commenced then, commenced when this government had decided that fruit-growing was still to have something approaching to a fair measure of protection in common with other Canadian industries. In 1901, ten short years ago, our industry was still small,
567,000	trees representing the orchards of that far west. We have had the faith and energy to build it up under conditions more expensive r nd difficult than those ever faced in oUier fruit-growing districts of Canada We have had to bear the enormous cost of clearing land of our heavy timber and immense outlays in engineering works for irrigation purposes.
I may point out to lion, members that in one valley alone, the Okanagan, $1,500,000 have already been spent in irrigation works for orchard purposes and vast outlays of the same kind are going on all over the province at the present time. We have had, and yet have, unusual difficulties in transportation, owing not a little to the mountainous character of the whole country. We have had, in addition, always a scarcity of labour, with a corresponding high remuneration. We have had little or no help in procuring more labour or additional settlers. I might Tefer ministers to a speech in this House in 1907 delivered by the former member for Yale-Cariboo, in which he pointed out to the government which he supported that they had done nothing to assist in solving this problem. Yet, Sir, in spite of these things, we have progressed to an extent that in the past ten years we have increased our orchards one thousand ner cent, and to-day have
5,000,000 trees. It is a record that should be a source of pride, not onlv to ourselves, but io every true Canadian who realizes that the sound development of the Pacific-coast province is as vital to the welfare of the nation as the development of the east. But although we have made rapid progress we are still only in the beginning of things. Immense tracts of land are in process of

being subdivided, and of being turned into more orchards. As yet but a small percentage of our trees are in bearing. Thousands of men have spent their all in the expensive work of bringing their small holdings to a stage when they will see some reward for their labours, and it is a deplorable and cruel proposal put forward by this government, for the wiping out of' the moderate tariff assistance now in force can be described in no other terms.
What is our position? Our natural, our great market is in the Canadian prairies. We face there competition from our sister province Ontario, whose friendly rivalry we do not deplore. But we face, also, a much more dangerous and fierce competition from the Pacific coast states. Absolutely no argument can be advanced to show that British Columbia has an equivalent in the form of a market in those states. Their markets are glutted with their awn products, and each of the great fruit-producing states is exporting an enormous annual surplus. California, besides her vast exports of citrus fruits, exported this last year 14,050 cars of such fruits as we grow in British Columbia and Ontario. A careful estimate of existing conditions indicates a twenty per cent increase in their output annually for the next few years. I submit an extract from a report carefully prepared by the chief of the horticultural department in British Columbia dealing with production last year:
Apricots-Wenatchee	valley, 300 cars,
Yakima valley, 12 cars, other producers, 15 cars.
This is in the state of Washington alone.
Peaches-Wenatchee valley, 300 cars, Yakima valley, 1,000 cars, other districts in Idaho and Washington, 300 cars. Total, 1,600 cars.
The tremendous preponderance of these districts in peaches over British Columbia districts resulted in a had glut and low prices this year. In plums the American side produces principally the Italian prune. The Williamette valley put up 200 cars of the dried article. Washington valleys shipped 100 cars of the fresh fruit, and southern Idaho shipped 450 to 500 cars. This latter district broke the market for British Columbia prunes and made the season, while not disastrous, one of quite low prices.
Apples-Yakima valley, actual shipment about 2,800 cars. Wenatchee, 2.000 cars. Walla Walla and Dayton not quite 400 cars. Mood river, 500.
And many other similar returns from the innumerable well established fruit valleys of the whole of the northwest states.
In apples the tremendous production indicated above broke the market latterly.
The market referred to is our own prairie country.
And No. 1 Rome Beauties are being offered in Calgary laid down at $1.45, which equals
$1.10 in the Okanagan valley for high class fruit. The total yield in the States west of the Rockies, including Colorado, this year was close to 15,000 cars.
A typical illustration of these valleys is that of Yakima, in Washington. A recent sketch in the ' World of To-day ' magazine contains the following:
Yakima valley is 200 miles long. The Yakima river extending through the valley irrigates the immense orchards. The acreage in full bearing is relatively small, but there are in different stages of bearing about 18,000 acres principally apples, peaches and pears. There are at present 45,000 acres set to fruit and the acreage adapted is fully double that now planted. The shipments for 1910 are upwards of 5,000 carloads of which 3,000 carloads are apples.
Now Sir, the tale of this great horticultural field in the western states might be extended, but I have already given the House a sufficient idea of the standing of our competitors. With this enormous output, it is obvious that profitable markets are a matter of keen anxiety to the United States. And here I might read part of a speech of President Taft as showing why they want these markets and why, from their point of view, this agreement should be put through. President Taft said:
We have, with pioneer energy, pushed on to the Pacific, and taken up all the good land. We are now spending millions to reclaim the arid and semi-arid lands of the great western desert.
They are reclaiming- these lands_for _th_e purpose of extending their fruit ranches.
Should we not, by taking down a useless and unnecessary tariff wall, bring within our agricultural resources the great plains of the Canadian Northwest?
In other words: Should not we get this duty removed in order that we m_ay get the enormous Canadian market in the Northwest.
The United States secured for the farmers the free listing of such important agricultural products as cottonseed oil, all kinds of fruits and vegetables, timothy and clover seeds, eggs, and numerous other products in which the movement to Canada from the United States is much greater than from Canada to the United States.
I think it is absolutely clear what President Taft intended, and what is the knowledge on this particular matter of the men on the other side of the line.
The transportation rates of Washington and Oregon to Winnipeg are as favourable, if not more so, than out own. American capital is already quite heavily interested in the wholesale trade in the western provinces. The wholesalers who have American connections, keep in constant touch with the shipping houses and pack-

ing firms of Washington and Oregon. The highest class fruit is customarily shipped eastwards to the big American cities, to which they get a more ready access than we could ever hope for. The tremendous surplus is forcing its way into our own market, competing against our No. 1 stock and often beating down our prices to _ a point none too profitable for us, but which their growers accept rather than get nothing. Much of the fruit is bought outright f.o.b., on the American side, but Sir, in addition to the great quantity of ears handled in this way, there were this last season, 95 cars sent into our prairie markets on consignment-not ordered, but literally dumped-the growers of Washington and Oregon prepared to take whatever a commission house could procure. These conditions obtain with a duty of 13 cents a case on apples, 20 cents a case on peaches and 10 cents a case on plums. What will happen when that duty is wiped out ? I need not point out that the danger to the Ontario and especially to the British Columbia, producer, is not only the loss of the amount of the duty, but the fiercer competition from those large and ever-growing areas which will naturally deflect a far greater volume of their products when even that slight barrier is swept away. If it is retorted that we have just as good a country and should be able to hold our own on equal terms, I can but reply that the terms at the present time are not equal. To say nothing of the handicap which a business in its constructive stage must always have as against a powerful rival fiTmly established. I may point out that our costs of production are greater than those of our southern competitor. I again quote from a careful report made to our Provincial Association:
In the Rogue river valley, Southern Oregon, a team costs $4 to $5 per day, as against our $6 and $7. Day labour is from $1.50 up to $1.75 as against our $2.50. The average cost of packing apples is 6 to 7 cents a box as against our 8 to 10 cents. The boxes themselves cost 10 to 11 cents as against our 14 cents. In the apple districts of eastern Washington prices are somewhat in advance of these, but as a rule prices for labour and boxes are 25 per cent cheaper than in British Columbia. Our selling prices, however, must be based on those of our competitors who are operating under those more favourable conditions.
Mr. Speaker, I have endeavoured to place the claims and the position of the British Columbia producer as fairly as I could before the House. It is the same position that was taken in 1907 when the last tariff revision took place, a revision which slightly increased the fruit duties. At that time the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson), remarked that it was a tariff Mr. BURRELL
which applied to the whole Dominion of Canada and he urged members to look upon it from the standpoint from which the Finance Minister felt it to be his duty to look at it-that is-and I quote his exact words (Hansard 1907): ' to see what he could do that would be fair to all parts of the country.' No further hearing was given to the fruit-growing interests before this blow fell. There was a bare possibility that our fruit interest might be endangered by pressure from Washington and accordingly, the Ontario Fruit Growers' Association at a representative meeting in Toronto on November 17 last, passed the following resolution:
Resolved, that in view of the possible negotiations with the United States in regard to reciprocity of tariffs, the Ontario Fruit Growers' Association wish to put on record our unqualified disapproval of any reduction in the duties on fruit coming into Canada without consulting a committee to be appointed by this association, the same being now much lower on an average than the duties on manufactured goods and lower than they ought to be in view of the fact that there can be no monopoly or combine in fruits, the prices being fixed absolutely by the law of supply and demand within the Dominion, which contains ample territory suitable to produce in the utmost profusion all the fruits that the country can consume for at least many decades to come, which insures that the consumer cannot be injured in the long run, and the fruit industry can be extended _ in proportion to the growth of the population with some assurance of a permanent market at home.
Now, Sir, I desire to call the attention of the House particularly to two points in connection with this matter. The Prime Minister hinted to the delegation of fruit growers the other day that they were too late, that their views should have been made known when the western farmers' delegation presented their case on December 16. Sir, this very resolution which I have read was forwarded to the Minister of Customs, and he acknowledged receipt of it, on December 15, the day before the western farmers were heard. But, Sir, the report of the western farmers' meeting, the report which I hold m my hand, contains a resolution specifically setting forth the views of the fruit growers along the very lines of the other resolution which I have read. I will not read the resolution, it can be found in the earlier part of this report, and is from the Niagara District Fruit Growers' Association, and is along the same lines. It was brought before this House, or telegraphed, on the same day. Does the Prime Minister think that these subterfuges were creditable to him? Did he think they were likely to deceive those men who came up here? Should it ever be too late to keep faith? Should it ever be too late to fulfil promises? Should it ever be too

late to do justice to the people of this country? Now, in addition to the resolution to which I have referred, there was another one passed almost a year ago by the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association. On January 7, before these proposals were put into effect, the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association, in annual convention, passed this resolution:
That this representative meeting of British Columbia fruit growers is absolutely opposed to any reduction on fruit entering Canada, as such action will undoubtedly result in great loss to the fruit industry here in its present stage of development.
Now, when I was speaking here last night, urging upon the Minister of Customs that the condition of the fruit industry had not altered since 1907, except in the direction of making a still stronger case, the minister took a rather curious stand. Hon. gentlemen who were here will remember that he interrupted me and claimed that I was not fair in my presentation, and that the conditions were different, as we would now have free entry into the United States. In all, or nearly all, the resolutions recently dealt with, the consistent plea is for retention of our duty. Where we have asked for equalization or revision, it has been for revision upwards on a scale something like that of the United States. Equalization by the abolition of all duties would not be equalization, but it would be the absolute destruction of those interests. No fruit grower ever dreamed of abolishing the Canadian duties. Why, Sir, the minister was there for the express purpose of guarding those interests. If he, who should have known the facts, has allowed himself to be over-reached, or to be out-played by the great fruit interests of the United States, upon him and upon this government the responsibility must rest, and for ourselves we can only regard it as the most culpable negligence on their part. I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Customs to this point.

speechtext: I verv much regret that the Minister of Customs is not in his place, the Minister of Finance is not in his place, and the Prime Minister is not here either, when a great national industry is being menaced with destruction. I am glad my hon. friend has called attention to the fact that they are absent. I must sav that when the only fruit grower in this House, representing this enormous industry, is doing his level best to put a moderate and fair presentation of the case before the House, and to protest against the proposal to destroy this industry, one of these ministers ought to be in his place to listen to the case. speechtext:
Well, I move, then-Ah, here is the minister. Now, Mr. Chairman, that we have got one of these gentlemen back in his seat, I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Customs to a point which he did not seem to understand last night. I regret, of course, that he has not been able to follow me when I quoted the resolutions which bore on that matter, but if he will carefully read the various resolutions to which I have referred, lie will note that the one from the Ontario Fruit Growers' Association, which he received and acknowledged the day before the western farmers'' delegation came here, plainly put on record its ' unqualified disapproval of any reduction of duties,' and it states that the duties are now ' lower than they ought to be.' The resolution from the Niagara district, to which I have referred also, urges that the present duties, if continued, will be to the advantage of the country. The whole argument is against the abolition of duty. The British Columbia resolution urges in positive terms that no reduction be made. Now, Sir, these protests came to this government before the reciprocity proposals were known, and since the nature of these proposals has become known to every industry of Canada, and since the intention of the government has been disclosed, the government is aware that petition after petition, resolution after resolution, have been sent in, and all these are along the same lines, deprecating a reduction of duty, and pointing out the grave nature of the injury to the fruit industry of British Columbia especially. I have many of them here, and not a day passes without more of them coming. Here is one from a district where the fruit interests are as great as those of the whole province of Nova Scotia. I refer now to the valley of the Okanagan. I received this letter only yesterday, and there is with it a resolution from the Associated Boards of Trade of the Okanagan valley. I call upon the Minister of Customs, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Inland Revenue, who have all been down in that district, to pay par-

ticular attention to this resolution. I received this yesterday, but it was dated five or six days ago:
Associated Boards of Trade for the Okanagan Valley.
Office of the Secretary, Vernon, B.C.
Copy of Resolution.
That the Associated Boards of Trade for the Okanagan Valley at their annual meeting now assembled urged in the strongest manner upon the Dominion government the absolute necessity of maintaining the present import duty on fruit as from the United States.
The fruit industry in British Columbia is in the infant stage with great possibilities which has been stated by responsible men will equal the lumber industry of the province, and at present stage requires careful handling and fostering. There are millions of dollars invested in the fruit industry in the province more than in the farm implement business of Ontario which has been nursed and protected; by so doing these factories of Canada are classed in this line as the leading industries of the world. Without this protection through their growing years these magnificent plants now employing thousands would never have existed. The same applies to the British Columbia fruit industry in which the growers have invested many millions of dollars, besides the very large investments of capital in irrigation systems running into millions of dollars.
The necessity of a protection duty outside the fostering of a young and promising industry, is the undeniable fact that the natural market for British Columbia, ' The Northwest Territories ' is made the dumping ground for surplus fruit from the Northwestern States which already possess a large and fully developed fruit industry and the pernicious action of consignment is resorted to on a large scale. It is well taken that the fruit growers are entitled to have their rights guarded the same as has been the case for other enterprises.
Now. the Prime Minister knows something of the development in that country. The Minister of Agriculture lias been over a considerable portion of the fruit districts of British Columbia. He stayed in the great peach district along the Okanagan lake. He knows, or ought to know, what positive and direct injury and discouragement will be inflicted on that section of British Columbia. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) told the House the other day that as a bachelor he had great difficulty in living on $9,500.

Did not the minister sav that while he could live on $9,500 a Mr. BURRELL
year it was very difficult, indeed, fo? a minister with a family to properly support that family on that income?

speechtext:
ment of fruit-growing and the farming population. If I did believe that a savage hunt for the dollar was the dominating principle of our life-that every man and every province -would ruthlessly pursue their own interests absolutely regardless of the hurt to others-that the knife was to be plunged into a Canadian brother for the sake of personal gain, then, Sir, I should indeed despair of our citizenship and could but say: God help this confederation which was built up on very different and very much more noble principles.
Sir, why did British Columbia enter confederation ? There was much to lose, there was much opposition-but the deep-rooted, the passionate desire to see a great highway from east to west, in order that scattered peoples holding the same traditional faiths, might become one nation, overcame every obstacle. The echoing thunder of the first transcontinental train as it swept through the Fraser canyon to the Pacific coast, meant much for Canada. It meant not only that it was possible for east to trade with west, it stood for the close linking of province to province, of brother to brother, in ties of sentiment as well as ties of commerce.
I have said we lost much. That is too long a story to tell now, but I may remind the House that, owing to the exceptional and difficult character of our great mountainous country, we have faced a burden of administrative expenditure utterly out of proportion to any other province in the Dominion. We received an absolutely inadequate compensation- financially, and that fact has been recognized, though somewhat late in the day, by the Prime Minister. But I will say to the Minister of Finance especially, that we in British Columbia accepted the responsibilities, the obligations, the burdens of confederation, though we have tried and shall still try to get them honourably and equitably adjusted. But the Minister of Finance' with less reason, with far less justification than ourselves, was the man, who himself, preached a fiery and bitter crusade throughout his own province, with disruption of confederation as his text. He, of all men, knowing at least something of our difficulties, should be the last man in Canada to add another pound to our burden._ My right hon. friend, the Prime Minister, cherishes a grievance against British Columbia. He has himself to blame for the fact that the whole province is solidly arrayed against him. But, Sir, additional injustice meted out to the people of the far west is not the way to heal old wounds. No one should know better than the Prime Minister, that the alienation of a whole province is a bitter and irrefutable proof that his government has not dealt justly with British Columbia. No additional Mr. BURRELL
harshness of treatment can strengthen my right hon. friend's hold on the popular heart, it will lead inevitably to the further weakening of himself and his party throughout Canada.	_
Sir, this is a movement, confessedly initiated by the United States for their own purpose. It is in some respects a ceding of our own control over our own destiny. If consummated, it will loosen and not tighten existing ties between province and province. We who have for years purchased hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of products from our prairie friends will find ourselves compelled to buy from the immediate south, from the foreign producer. It does irreparable harm to our interprovincial trade-it lessens the national feeling of the people of Canada and turns their energies in new directions. It means the exploiting of our natural resources and raw materials by a people who will expend their own energies and labour in the varied work of turning out the finished article. If it is an economic truth that every import must be paid for by an export, then our natural products, finding their market in the United States, will soon be paid for by a great flow of their manufactured goods.
If it has a shattering effect on our interprovincial trade and puts a new face on our national life, it also foreshadows possible changes in our political future. I have only to allude to the item in to-day's paper, already referred to, the statement that the annexation of Canada, was the keynote of Mr. Clarke, Speaker of the House, in whipping the members of_ his party into line in support of the reciprocity agreement. Not once or twice, but thrice, did he boldly declare: We are preparing to annex Canada. In the light of these words, there is some ground for that noble and passionate appeal in the closing words of the speech delivered yesterday by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), who said:
This is our land, and please God we will keep it for our children and our children's children. This proposal cuts square across our national ideas and will endanger them. We should think well before entering upon it. The path we are about to enter leads from home; it should not be entered upon lightly.
I do not say that we in British Columbia are more imperial, more anxious than our fellow Canadians in other provinces to strengthen the bonds which bind us to the mother country, but British Columbia, of all the great provinces which form this confederation, would be most loth to see any step taken which would conceivably end in sharing the political future of that great country to the south, and in this proposal, we see nothing that strengthens
362ft

the grip of hands across the sea, but much that weakens it. The pact was unnecessary, the arrangements as a whole, have dangerous tendencies, and the scheme involves a grave injustice to one large body of Canadian producers and citizens.
No redress for plain grievances. No remedies for obvious injuries; take it or leave it, says the government. Have it all, or have none. Sir, I say for myself then, and I think I speak for my constituents too, 1 want none of it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, like every hon. mem her in this House I realize the magnitude and the importance of the question now before you and the great influence which it will, in all human probability, exert upon the future of this country. I happen, in this debate, to follow my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo (Mr. Burrell) who has devoted by far the greater part of his remarks, to one particular branch of the subject, namely the effect of the present proposals upon the fruit industry in this country. I do not for a moment claim to have the knowledge of my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo either in regard to fruit or in regard to general conditions in British Columbia. It was, I believe, arranged that my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Ralph Smith), who is at present indisposed and has sickness in his family, should reply to the speech of the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo, and I think that I had better leave that task to my hon. friend -from Nanaimo^who expects shortly to be present again in his seat. But there are a great many general principles involved in this question which can be, and should be discussed by members from the various sections of Canada, not as they pertain to local or special interests, but as they bear upon the whole trade and future development of this great country. This is the eleventh session that I have had the honour of occupying a seat in this House. I represent a riding in the central portion of western Ontario having a population equally divided between rural and urban. The whole county of Wellington may be said to be a fair average of the counties in the western portion of the province. Its industries are similar to those of neighbouring counties such as Waterloo, Oxford, Perth, Brant, Huron, Grey, Bruce, Duff^ erin and other counties. These are all to a considerable extent manufacturing counties, but to a very much larger extent agricultural counties. The agriculture carried on in my own county is not the agriculture which is carried on in the west. It is not to any large extent a grain-producing county. What grain we do produce is largely consumed in the feeding of livestock, which may be said to be the leading farm operation of the county. Consequently the county of Wellington is very greatly interested in the proposals now before the Chair. The grain we produce is fed to a high-bred class of cattle. We raise beef cattle for the supply of the local market, the Toronto market, and very largely, at certain times of the year, the Ottawa market ; 'but by far the larger portion of our cattle industry is concerned with foreign markets. We have in the county of Wellington a large class of purebred cattle, sheep, hogs and poultry. A casual drive through any part of the county of Wellington during the summer time would serve as an eye-opener to many people in regard to the conditions as they exist among the rural population of that county. I would like to take my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) on a short trip through the riding of South Wellington, and let him see the class of people who are engaged in the great farming industry there. I realize that these proposals affect my constituents directly. I realize also that I represent a city population of 16,000 people, living in the city of Guelph, as well as five villages, each containing some manufacturing industry besides the ordinary village population. I believe that the various classes of the population are all vitally interested in these proposals ; and, having given them my best consideration and judgment, I have come to the conclusion that it is of the greatest interest to the county from which I come, and to all counties similarly situated in the western portion of the province _of Ontario, that this measure be adopted by this House.
In this instance I desire to follow the lead and the good example set by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition in dealing with this question. He discussed it in what I consider the best parliamentary form-not from the standpoint of party politics at all ; but be gave us what I assume was from his point of view his reasoned judgment-his conclusions and the reasons for those conclusions ; and while I do not agree with him, I do not think I can do better than follow his manner and method in presenting my case to the House. I may say also for the hon. member of the opposition who also preceded me (Mr. Martin Burrell), that he argued his case from his point of view without that asperity, that bitterness, which we frequently have in this House over questions which should be argued rather on their merits. I regret that I cannot endorse or approve of the method adopted by my hon. friend from North Toronto, who,
I am sorry to see, is not in his place this afternoon. It might be the part of presumption for me to offer any suggestions to the hon. member for North Toronto is to parliamentary style or as to the method or . manner of presenting his ease ; but were

he in his seat I would tell him that if his speech were stripped of its rhetoric, if the feathers and the plumage were taken from it, and we came down to the facts he presented and the arguments he sought t; make, we would find that the speech was perhaps the most meagre and insubstantial that he has delivered in this House. I hope to be able to show before I conclude that some of the arguments he presented are absolutely without foundation, or, if they have a foundation, he certainly did not reveal that foundation to the House. Some of them are ridiculous and some of them absolute absurdities. I believe that the hon. member for North Toronto himself realized that, and hence we find him, in his best declamatory style, a style of parliamentary eloquence which during the last half-century has, I think, rather dropped out-if not in this House, certainly in the Imperial House of Commons, where all that they ask is the facts and the arguments, waiving the declamation.
It has been said in this debate that it would be well for the government to withdraw this measure for the present. It has been suggested that the House has not had sufficient information on the subject. I take issue with that statement. This question has been very prominently before Canada for a year at least, since March, 1910, in the newspapers, on the platforms, in political arguments at various places. Every man of ordinary intelligence knew that it would be a subject for discussion in this House, and I am sure that hon. members of this House have canvassed the situation and canvassed it pretty thoroughly. That of course was only as the question presented itself in abstract form, but since the 26th January last, we have had it presented in concrete form, with all the details and information necessary to enable us to give it full consideration and form an independent and calm judgment upon it. The ordinary channels have been open to all hon. members. We have been educated by the press, by the representations of deputations, by communications from our constituents and by petitions of various kinds, and we have had at our disposal a very complete summary of the whole case in the tariff blue-book handed to the House some ten days ago, so that if any hon. gentleman should complain that he has. not sufficient information on the subject, I can only say that he has not shown the necessary energy and perseverance, because otherwise he would have had all the information he could possibly desire to enable him to pass an intelligent judgment on the question. It has been said also that there is no demand for any such measure. Where is the demand, has been asked? Whence does it come? Why, it almost seems waste of time to answer such a question, but for the purpose of my argument I desire to do Mr. GUTHRIE.
so; and I state without hesitation that there has not been a period in this country since 1866 down to the present year of grace when there has not been a positive demand in Canada for better trade relations with the United States. And that demand has not been a dormant one, but one made public in many ways and on many occasions. Nor has it been the demand of one political party or one political leader, but from every government and from the whole population of Canada; and I desire, even at the expense of a few moments of our valuable time, to relate something of the history of that demand.
In the first place the old reciprocity treaty was abrogated in 1866. Sir Alexander Gault and Sir William Howland representing Canada, and Mr. Smith and Mr. Henry representing Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, proceeded to Washington and remained there a couple ot weeks before the abrogation and pleaded to get a new treaty. In this they failed. Confederation came in 1867, and our first tariff Act in 1868 expressed our demand for reciprocity by containing a clause stating our readiness to enter into such a treaty. In 1869 another demand was made on Washington by the government of Sir John Macdonald. That government despatched Sir John Rose to Washington to obtain reciprocity, but he also failed. In 1871, I think it was, another deputation went to Washington, headed by Sir John Macdonald, when the treaty of Washington was negotiated, and again a demand was made for reciprocity and again refused. The government of Mr. Alexander Mackenzie, which came into office in 1874, sent -a deputation to Washington with Hon. George Brown at its head. As the result of their mission, a draft treaty was submitted to the Senate of the United States which that body refused to pass. In 1879, there came a change of government, and the tariff policy of the Conservative government contained a statutory offer to the United States for reciprocal tariff legislation or reciprocity. Then we come down to 1891 when Sir John Macdonald put himself on formal record in regard to that matter in his address to the electors of that year a copy of which has recently been published in the Montreal ' Gazette.' Commenting on the policy of the Libera] oarty of that day, he said of the policy of the Conservative party towards the United States.
We are perfectly willing to trade with you on equal terms. We are desirous of having a fair reciprocity treaty, but we will not consent to open our markets to you while yours remain closed to us.
In 1891, after the Conservative victory at the polls, we had another deputation going to Washington, and on this deputation, was

my hon- friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) then Minister of Finance. Nothing again was accomplished. The American authorities still turned a deaf ear to our requests, and these gentlemen were not able to make any impression on them. In 1893 was held the great Liberal convention in this city of Ottawa in which a reciprocity plank was placed in the iplatifonn as one of the things which the Liberal party would attempt to obtain if returned to power. They were returned in 1896, and in 1898 sent a deputation to Washington for the very purpose of securing a reciprocity treaty. That deputation also failed in its mission.
That then is the record up to 1899 of both parties with regard to reciprocity with the United States. Now the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says that in the year 1899 the leader of the present government, the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), declared in this House and afterwards in England that he had turned his back on Washington, that he would no longer seek reciprocity with the United. States, but that he would endeavour to make trade arrangements with the rest of the world and particularly the British Empire. Well, there is this to be said, that my right hon. friend was the first Prime Minister of Canada who took that dignified stand with regard to negotiations with Washington. Previous governments had made offers and had been refused, and sometimes the refusal was not couched in the most polite terms, as my hon. friend from - North- Toronto (Mr. Foster) could tell us if he would. The only proper, dignified, statesmanlike course to pursue was that taken by the right hon. the leader of this government. If any further attempts, he declared, were made to obtain reciprocity, the offer would have to come from Washington and not from Canada. We waited many years during which we made no further demand or request, nor did any come from them, but at the end of ten years a request did come from Washington, and at the end of eleven years that request is now before the House in concrete form. In the face of these facts, how can the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) or the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), argue that there has not been a positive demand in this country for such a measure since 1866.
My hon. friend the leaaer of the opposition says that times have changed, that we are now in the year 1911, and not in 1866, and that conditions have changed. True they^ have, but neither geographical nor climatic conditions have changed. The nature of our products has not changed nor has the character of the products of the United States, but our lines of transportation east and west and north and 115
south have been perfected, and if there was good reason for a demand for reciprocity in 1866, there is just as good or better in the year 1911.
Just a word as to the proposal itself. The proposal does not come in the form of a treaty, and I think it is well that it does not. Had it been m the torm ot a hard and fast binding treaty for 25 or 50 years, i could have seen some torce in me argument that we had tied our hands and could not enter into reciprocal arrangements with other countries and could not improve our relations within the empire with regard to trade matters, it came in the form of a simple international bargain based on good faith. I think that is one of the best features of the measure as presented to the House. The terms of the measure can all be taken from ia single clause in the letter addressed by the hon. Minister o.f Finance and the Minister of Customs to the Secretary of State of the United States, on the 21st January, 1911. These are the words :
Nevertheless, it is distinctly understood that we do not attempt to bind for the future the action of the United States Congress or the parliament of Canada, but that each of these authorities shall be absolutely free to make any change of tariff policy or of any other matter covered by the present arrangement that may be deemed expedient.
Surely, that is clear, plain and simple; and it is a statement which is formally confirmed by the letter of the Secretary of State of _the United States. And that is air the bargain or agreement between the two countries at this time.
Now, treaties may be good at times and they may be bad at times. Treaties do involve, sometimes, international entanglements of an unforseen kind. Treaties sometimes involve or cause subsequent embarrassments. A treaty made between a country having the wealth and population of the United States on the one hand and Canada on the other hand might, some day, prove an embarrassment to this country and an embarrassment to Ureat Britain. So, if my opinion is worth anything, I give my opinion that the present arrangement, based on the mutual good faith of both countries, and, as we hope, for the mutual advantage, of both countries, is the best possible arrangement, so tar as Canada is concerned, in the way of reciprocal trade arrangement with the United States.
It has been argued: Wiiy do not you wait until the colonial conference has met in London this year; something new may be developed there, something new may be evolved. The answer is that we have not made any hard and fast treaty; no binding arrangement has been made; our hands



are not tied, our hands are free; and, if anything better for the interests of Canada shall be developed or evolved at the colonial conference, Canada is perfectly free to take advantage of it. These are the reasons which lead me to the conclusion that the present arrangement, resting as it does on a mutual bargain, is by all means the best form in which to put an arrangement with the United States.
It has been said by some that Canada has ail the best of the bargain and hy others that Canada has all the worst of the bargain. I do not believe that arguments of that kind will appeal to any reasonable man. A bargain has always two sides to it, and unless the advantage of the arrangement be mutual, it will not last a twelve month. We cannot have it all our own way, the other contracting party must have some of the advantages. It is very much as was said by David Harum in the book of that name: ' When you make a horse trade, it is always well to let the other fellow get something out of it.' I do not think that a one-sided bargain would have been of any advantage to us at an. But what I do say is that the arrangement presented before us will give Canada tremendous advantages over the position which she now occupies, and, on the other hand, I am ready to admit that the United States may get some advantage also. But I do think that the advantage preponderates on the side of Canada very, very largely.
In order to place my case connectedly before the House, I would like to examine the trade position of Canada to-day? I do not intend to impose a lot of figures on the House, and I shall only refer to them in round numbers and as rapidly as I can; but I think that it is necessary, if one is to have a proper appreciation of the effect of the present proposal, to have regard to our present conditions. I find that the total trade of Canada of last year, exports and imports, amounted to $693,000,000: based on home consumption, $649,000,000. And the astonishing, even startling, fact is that $580,000,000 of our total trade is done with the United Kingdom and the United States. Our export and import trade with Great Britain is $245,000,000, and our export and import trade with the United States, $336,000,000. In other words, 9U per cent of our whole foreign trade is done with two countries and only ten per cent with the rest of the world. As this trade proposal or agreement affects the trade with our two best customers, it is of far more consequence that we should scan it very carefully to see that in what we may now do we injure neither our trade with the one nor our trade with the other of them.

speechtext:
It is well also to note the nature of the trade we have with Great Britain, and the nature of the trade we have with the United States. From Great Britain we import $95,000,000 worth of goods, and to Great Britain we export $149,000,000 worth. From the United States we import $223,000,000 worth and to the United States we export $113,000,000 worth. In other words, Great Britain buys from us 54 per cent of all our exports, but the United States buys from us 40 per cent of our exports. Great Britain sells to us 20 per cent of all our imports, and the United States sells to us 60 per cent of all our imports. Now, it is frequently said that the balance of trade, as between Canada and the United States, is entirely against Canada. It is also argued and urged- and was urged by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax)-that we have given Great Britain no real preference at all, that all we ever gave was a sham preference, a pure fiction. I must say that, on the tariff rates which my hon. friend gave to the House, and which I believe to be approximately correct, there is, apparently, a discrimination against Great Britain in favour of the United States. But I think the leader of the opposition should have been candid enough to give the reason, because he knows the reason and knows that the discrimination is not a real discrimination but an apparent one. You may examine the rates of duty which we charge in Canada, and you will find in the Trade and Commerce report, page 15, the following average rates: On all imports entering Canada from all countries, the average rate is 16/416; on all dutiable imports coming into Canada from all countries, 26-713. On all imports coming from Great Britain, the average rate is 18-914; on all dutiable imports from Great Britain the average rate is 25-107. On all imports from the United States, the average rate is only 13-570 and on all dutiable imports from the United States, the rate is 24-837. And the difference on total imports as between the United States and Great Britain on goods coming into Canada, is now 5J per cent in favour of the United States, and the average difference on all dutiable imports is one-fourth of one per cent, or 25 cents on $100 in favour of the United States. So that there is an apparent discrimination in favour of the United States and not a preference for Great Britain. But, as I say, it is apparent and not real. The reason for it is not hard to find. The reason for the apparent discrimination is to be found in tne list ofl free imports. On our total imports from Great Britain, amounting to $95,000,000, only $23,000,000 came in on the free list.
FEBRUARY Is, 1911
On our total imports from the United States, amounting to $223,000,000, over $98,000,000 come in on the free list.
When you average the free and the dutiable goods together, an apparent discrimination in favour of the United States appears, because the United States supplies to us so much of our free imports. Well, some one says, why don't you buy them from England? Why do you buy them from the United States? The reason is obvious, and if any one will glance ovetr the trade and navigation returns of this country he cannot fail to be struck with the reason almost in the first two or three pages of that report. Of the free imports I will take only a few of the large items. The imports of corn amount to $4,600,000; we get that all direct from the United States free, and it is not produced in, nor is it exported from, Great Britain. We want it .here to feed our hogs and cattle. Hon members will remember that prior to 1896, under the Conservative government, the farmers paid 7 cents a bushel to get that corn to feed their stock. I wish the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) was here now, because I never look at that corn item without thinking of the anomaly which he permitted to exist in the government of which he was Finance Minister. He charged the farmers 7 cents a bushel to bring in corn to feed to their export cattle, and he allowed the distillers to bring in corn free to make whisky for export purposes.
- Mr. SPROULE, Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question? If I understand him correctly, he said that there was an apparent difference in favour of the United States, but it was only apparent, and he gave the free imports from Great Britain and the United States to show that the duty charged against the United States was only apparent. But leaving out the free imports entirely, when he considers the dutiable goods separately, the balance is really in favour of the United States; in other words, the duty was a little lower against the United States than against Great Britain.

speechtext: That is correct; I will come to that.

speechtext: If that be so, is it not real?
