speechtext:
No, it is not, as I will show presently. Do not anticipate me. Before I leave that question of importing corn for the distillers, I must say that after a time that anomaly in the tariff was removed. The people in my county who imported dutiable corn to manufacture export cattle did not like their neighbours in the adjoining county of Waterloo to have the privilege of importing free corn for the manufacture of export whisky, and the 1151
present junior judge of the county of Wellington informs me that he, as the leading prohibitionist of this House on the Conservative side, called the government's attention to it, and they took it off.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Which government did this?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
The government of which the hon. member for North Toronto was Finance Minister. The next item of importation of free raw material from the United States is anthracite coal and coke, amounting to $16,000,000. Then comes binder twine, $1,750,000, made free for the benefit of the farmers. Then comes manilla grass, or hemp, or fibre, $1,000,000, I think chiefly used in the penitentiaries. Then comes raw cotton, $9,360,000. That is not a product that England exports, but one that she imports in tremendous quantities. The next item is tropical fruits, $3,700,000. Then, crude rubber, and rubber sheets for manufacture in rubber factories, a little over four millions. Then lumber imported, chiefly hardwood, $8,000,000. Raw tobacco, $3,115,000; metal ores and minerals, $16,000,000. These are some of the items on the free list. You can go over the free list of goods imported into this country, and you will find that about seventy or seventy-five million dollars worth come in from the United States free of duty which are not the product of Great Britain at all, and are not goods that she exports.
Now, in regard to dutiable goods, there is an apparent discrimination of 25 cents on the hundred dollars, and how is that accounted for? It is accounted for by reason of this fact, that this government, -and, for aught I know, its predecessors, considered that the manufacturers of Canada should be allowed to bring in partly manufactured goods at nominal rates of duty, largely goods used m iron and steel industries. I know of goods coming into Guelph by the carload for the manufacture of an article of iron called skelp; it comes in sheets at the rate of five per cent, and comes in on the list of dutiable goods, but the duty is placed at a nominal amount.
If you look over the trade and navigation returns you will find item after item of this kind going into the manufacture of implements, into manufactures of hardware, and into the manufactures of various kinds of machinery, on which the rates run from as low as 2 to 5, 7 and 8 per cent. Then there is the matter of agricultural implements, on which the rate is only 17i per cent. Wo do not get any of these goods from England. So that in the general average there is an apparent discrimination in favour of the United States to the extent of 25 cents on the $100. But is that a test? Here is the test; Take goods that both countries manufacture and export, take goods of common manufacture which Canada buys from the United States and

Great Britain, and see whether there is a preference or not. Woollens or manufacture of woollens-last year we bought from Great Britain $19,000,000, and . from the United States $925,000. Is there not a 'discrimination in favour of Great Britain there? And so on with the other articles in this list :

Now, that, I submit, is the_ test. There are goods which both countries manufacture in their complete form and send into Canada, on which we have given a British preference of one-third less rate of duty on goods coming from Great Britain. Now, compare the sales made by Great Britain and the United States of that class of goods which they manufacture in common, and see whether there is a real preference or an imaginary one. I have only enumerated nine of the larger items, and I find that in the nine items the volume of imports from Great Britain is $42,000,000, and the volume of imports from the United States is $6,000,000. The United States goods come on an average five or six hundred miles, and Great Britain's goods come on an average of about 3.500 miles.
I am going to turn now to another definite question involved in the proposed arrangement. A great portion of the speech of the member for North Toronto yesterday and the day before, was directed to an effort to show that you are interfering with the British preference, and generally wiping that out, that you are interfering indeed with our imperial standing. I propose to show that we are not interfering with it, and I submit that he gave no facts that would convince any reasonable man that we are interfering with it. In the first place, I know that he has devoted time and attention to this subject. I know that he is a man very capable of examining this question from every point of view. I believe he has left no stone unturned. He has gene into it from top to bottom, turned if over and examined it. Taking his speech, as reported in ' Hansard,' at page 3405, I find he says that the total trade to be displaced or affected will be $95,000,000, that the arrangement will affect an import trade of $47,800,000 and an export trade of $47,300,000. I do not think his figures are collect, but I will, for the purpose of my argument, give my figures which are large-Mr. GUTHRIE.
ly in excess of the figures which he quoted; so that, if his argument be correct, it will be more correct and more imposing 'than the (presentation which he put (before the House. I do not know where he got his import figures, which, as given by the blue-book, are $40,000,000. Adding to that $650,000 for pulp wood and paper under a special item, the amount would be about $41,000,000. Then he places the imports which come to us under the schedules under discussion at $47,800,000. He has increased the amount by about 18 or 20 per cent, but 1 do nut know that that will make any difference in his argument. As I say, I 'do not know where he got his figures. 1 submit that the .present arrangement will not affect -merely $47,000.000 of our exports, but that the amount of our exports to be affected is the amount set out in the blue-book, called Tariff Relations, at page 68 and that is $205,000,000 and not $47,000,000 as stated by the hon. member for North Toronto. That $205,000,000 is made up of exports as follows:	To
Great Britain, $127,000,000; to the United States, $49,000,000; and to all other countries in the world, $28,000,000. Take these figures as set out in the blue-book, which are entirely favourable to the contention of my hon. friend, and arguing from that basis, let me show first the situation with regard to schedule 'A ' that, I know my hon. friend must have gone through from top to bottom, because he counted the items. He says there are 69 items in schedule ' A,' 39 of which have been untouched-not a very good word to express what he meant, a word that might be very misleading to many people. In regard to 30, he says the duty has been wiped out. What he means by 'untouched' I do not know. What he should have said was, that there was not any duty on them, because they have always been on the free list, and the other 30 articles have been placed on the free list. But, in looking over schedule ' A ' I found that there were 44, sections, subdivisions or groups, schedule ' A ' being the free list, and that 30 of these groups relate exclusively to natural products, that 11 of these groups relate exclusively to partly manufactured goods, which come into this country as raw material for the benefit of the manufacturer, and that only three of the articles under schedule ' A ' consist of manufactured goods. These three articles are (1) cream separators, which have always been free; (2) type setting machines of which we only got from Great Britain last year, $177 worth, and (3) paper, paper being a special item by itself. These are all the manufactured goods, included in this schedule. Cream separators always were free, and I do not know that they should always have been free, because I have been

down here with one or two deputations to get a duty put on them. I thought they were machinery just as much as other things were, or that they should properly be classed as agricultural implements, but the government persistently refused to place a duty on them. They always have been free and if they did come in from Great Britain, they would still come free. Type setting machines never did come from Great Britain, and as we only imported $177 worth last year, we could not have brought in any complete linotype machine. Wood pulp never came from Great Britain, but paper did. Paper to the extent of $7,302 came from Great Britain last year. What are our total imports under schedule * A '? Last year we received of goods now under schedule ' A ' $13,894,000 worth. Of that $13,000,000 worth we received from Great Britain, $4,-
190,000,	and from the United States $9,-
163,000.	One third of the goods coming into this country last year now under schedule 'A ' came from Great Britain and two thirds from the United States. The reduction in duty, by reason of the change and by reason of placing the thirty articles mentioned by the hon. member for North Toronto on the free list, will be, on the trade of last year, $1,400,000, or about 17J cents per head of our population, placing it at $8,000,000.
_ Now, my hon. friend's objection was that, you have injured the trade of Great Britain, that you have displaced the trade of Great Britain by the effect of your free )i-si. embraced in schedule ' A T am not going to the extent of quoting-Iris language: it can be found in ' Hansard.' It was ' a most extraordinary statement, and one for which he had not the slightest foundation. If we examine the list we must be convinced that the hon. member for North Toronto wanted to cover up the scanty foundation by a wealth of words, where he was at a loss for argument. What is that trade? We import from England $4,190,000 worth. It is nearly all made up of the single item of rolled iron and steel plates, amounting to $3,490,000. That is on the free list, but that always was in the free list and Great Britain sent that amount into Canada last year as a free article. Will that be displaced ?

speechtext: Yes.

I understand that it was a free article from Great Britain, and
I also thought it was free from the United States, but I will not be sure about that.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
That represents about seven eighths of the free list embraced in schedule ' A '. I am not going to take up all the items; I only propose to deal with the larger ones. The next item that I shall mention is that of grapes, of which we imported from Great Britain $104,000 worth. Every one knows, who knows anything about the kind of grapes we import from Great Britain, that they are the grapes that retail at $1.50 a pound, or $2.50 a bunch, and are not produced in Canada. They only had a duty of li per cent and the duty amounted to nothing in comparison with the value of the grapes. That trade will not be displaced. Then, we take vegetables and beans. Of vegetables, we imported $91,000 worth. These are not the vegetables we grow in Canada. I am informed that almost the whole value is represented by the one item of Spanish oniohs. which can only be produced in~tropical-countries and which are shipped into Canada via Great Britain. Another article is beans, by wdiich, they tell me, is meant Lima beans, which represent an import of $64,000. These are not produced in Canada; they come from South America and are shipped into Canada via Great Britain. Therefore, no trade will be affected with respect to these articles.
Take the argument of the hon. member for North Toronto, that when duties are reduced down to 10, 12 or 15 per cent, your preference amounts to nothing. I say that under that argument rolled iron and steel plates will come in from Great Britain just as freely as they came in before. These items that I have enumerated amount to almost the entire free list, as represented by schedule * A '. What is that to the total imports into this country from Great Britain-$4,191,000 out of a total of $95,000,000 ? In all probability,- indeed I wmuld stake my reputation upon it-in two or three years, as our purchasing power increases our purchases of goods under that same schedule ' A ' of w'hich we now buy $4,191,000 will be largely increased and not diminished.
Now, let me look at schedules ' B ' and

' D.' These are the schedules of goods on which there has been a tariff reduction. The total tariff reduction is $1,095,000, or about 124 cents per head upon the population of Canada, and if my estimate is correct it is about 3f per cent on the average. Now, is that going to seriously affect trade either with Great Britain or the United States? It cannot affect it with Great Britain because the duties are maintained at substantial amounts and Great Britain has one-third off that duty, which constitutes a decided preference. It cannot materially affect trade with the United States or imports from the United States because there is not enough reduction in any instance to allow American . manufacturers to compete with Canadian manufacturers. If we have today a duty of 30 per cent against the United States upon manufactured goods of any quality and it is reduced to 27 per cent, the increase of imports will he small at most because the reduction of duty has been small, and that argument applies to all the goods comprised in schedules ' B ' and * D.' What do sections ' B ' and ' D amount to? Last year all the goods enumerated in sections ' B ' and ' D ' imported into Canada amounted to $26,500,000. Of these we imported from the United States $23,196,000, and from Great Britain only $2,196,000. Our imports from Great Britain amounted to practically nothing, $2,196,000 out of $26,000,000 of goods included in these schedules. I maintain, and I think I can maintain it in the face of any argument, that there is every probability that next year and the year after, and the year after that we will have an annual increase in our purchases from Great Britain of the very goods mentioned in schedules ' B ' and ' D.' When you look at the scheduler of the goods that come in from Great Britain you will find they are made u.p nearly all of goods that sell on their own brand or patent. By reason of their inherent virtue they not only come into this country but in the face of a 40 per cent to 50 per cent duty they go into the United States and are sold there. The whole list comes to only $2,196,000. How is that made up? Biscuits and confectionery make up $522,000 in that list. Do you mean to say that one, or two, or three, or four cents duty will affect the sale in this country or in the United States of Huntley & Palmer's wares, made in Great Britain? Go into any large purveyor's store in New York like Park & Telford's, and see the magnificent display of Huntley & Palmer's biscuits and confectionery. They are there in the face of what? A duty of 40 per cent to 50 per cent. Is there any reason why they should not come into Canada in preference to any goods from the United States with one-third tariff advantage over the United States goods?
Take another large item, pickles, Crosse Mr. GUTHRIE.
& Blackwell, Lea & Perrin, Holbrooke, these are the names and brands that sell goods, and they sell them by reason of their inherent quality. They sell in the United States in the face of the highest kind of competition and of very stiff tariffs. Is there any reason to suppose that these goods will not come into Canada just as freely as before?
Then take cutlery, of which we import from Great Britain $223,854. People who know, or are supposed to know, tell me that English cutlery retains its place in the markets of Canada by reason of its brand, by reason of its name, its reputation and its inherent virtue. They tell me also that the cutlery from the United States never did have any large market in Canada, the chief competitor of British cutlery here being Germany, and Germany does not receive any advantage under this reciprocity arrangement with the United States. There is no reason to suppose that the cutlery imports from Great Britain will foe reduced one dollar if this arrangement is brought into force.	_
Imports of automobiles from Great Britain amount to $106,000. These are all controlled by patents and a man who wants an English motor car can get an English motor car, the question of dutv does not, as a rule, enter into the consideration.
Another item is musical instruments of which we import $118,000. They are sold largely on the reputation of the maker of the instrument. I think these are largely band instruments, and if English band instruments are better than American, and I believe they are, they will probably come in, in just as great quantifies or greater, because they still retain their one-third preference, and we will have far more purchasing power to buy musical instruments than we have had in the past.
I have gone over only a few items but if they are figured out they amount to almost three-quarters of our total imports under schedules ' B ' and ' D.' Will the hon. membeT for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) or any other member rise in his place and state as his considered judgment that the British manufacturers are going to be injured by schedules ' B ' and ' D.' Can they be injured? They will retain their position in regard to the tariff with their one-third preference. Nearly all goods mentioned in schedules ' B ' and ' D ' are sold by virtue of the reputation of the makers, by virtue of patents, trade marks, designs, &c. I think we have every reason to believe that a-s our prosperity grows we will import very much more of these same articles than we have ever imported in the past.
The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) grew very eloquent on the question and even went so far as to charge the Minister of Customs, not directly but indirectly,

with something like a breach of faith in a cablegram which he had sent to the Colonial office in Great Britain, setting forth that the proposed changes in the tariff between 'Canada and the United States would not interfere with the British preference. The statement made 'by Mr. Asquith, the Premier of Great Britain was :
The American-Canadian agreement had been carefully watched by the British Ambassador at Washington on behalf of British interests and he has been assured that, so far as British imports into Canada are concerned, the British preference would be scrupulously maintained.
I submit that that statement is true in substance and in fact, and I submit further that Mr. Bryce is perfectly satisfied on behalf of Great Britain with the arrangement that has been made. The official correspondence sets forth that Mr. Bryce was a party to it. Let me, in passing, read to the House a clipping which has been handed to me, taken from the Manchester ' Guardian,' a very influential paper published in Great Britain. It reads :
The whole policy of Mr. Bryce, the most successful British Ambassador at Washington in our generation, has been-if we may speak of an Ambassador's policy-directed towards drawing closer the bonds between Canada and the United States. He has been called the first Canadian Ambassador at Washington, and his policy has been in the best interests of Canada. But it has been governed primarily by British interests. Canada, in British world policy, is a gage of friendship between England and America. EnglancT gams a friend by every act that brings Canada into closer relations with the United States. There is no rivalry between England and the United States for the affections of Canada. She will best serve our policy by broadening the basis of her own prosperity and by a cordial policy of friendship with the United States.
Coming to the end of my argument on that point my statement is, and I am absolutely convinced in mv own mind that I am correct in what I state, that in no way, shape or form, in no way general or particular, are we interfering with British trade interests in Canada (by the proposals now before the Chair, and that if these negotiations when passed into law have any bearing whatever upon the status of British trade in Canada, it will be a beneficial _ effect, that our imports from Great Britain will not decrease ; there is no reason to make them decrease. As our prosperity increases, our imports from Great Britain will increase year after year. So that the action of the Minister of Financ -in sending his telegram, and the statement of the Premier of Great Britain founded on that telegram, were strictly in accordance with the facts.
Let me touch upon another of the more important points made by my hon. friend
from North Toronto. I do not know that I have ever heard in this House, during
an experience of eleven sessions, a more exaggerated statement of fact than was given to the House by one of its old members in the person of the hon. member for Nortli Toronto yesterday, when he referred to the effect of this treaty upon our natural resources and the inroads which were to be made upon them by American grabbers, American grafters and American millionaires. So far as I can see, the present proposal does not afford one shred of argument to support my hon. friend's noisy declaration in that respect. To dignify it, I might call it dogmatic assertion. It was more than that: it was deliberate exaggeration, because there is nothing in the proposed agreement to support it, and I will ask any hon. member opposite, as I would ask the hon. member for North Toronto if he were in his place, to stand up now and quote any statement on which that assertion was made.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: If there was nothing of that nature in it, why did President Taft say the other day that one of the great virtues of it was that it opened up the forests of British North America to the United States?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
My hon. friend either did not follow me or else he spoke too soon.
I say that there is nothing in this proposal to give the United States one whit of advantage in their access to our natural products that they have not had'during the last 50 years. We have not changed the status one iota. ITthe United States wanted our- lumber, our minerals, our fish, our wheat, or our live stock, all they had to do at any time during the last 50 years was to take off their tariff and come in and take them.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Then Mr. Taft must have been entirely wrong?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
The hon. member for North Toronto must have known these facts, because he has told the public of Canada time and again that the United States could obtain all the access they desired to our natural resources by dropping their tariff, and so they could. Yet he spent yesterday a whole hour in a laboured argument to show that there was nothing standing in the way of Canada if this treaty came into force, but devastation of our natural resources, that they would be taken to the United States, there manufactured into the finished product, and then shipped back to Canada. How could they come back to Canada under this treaty? Where is there any reduction in the schedules that would permit them? One branch of his argument is just as unfounded as the other. The United States, if they want our lumber, our minerals, our Wheat, or our cattle, will come here and pay for them. We are

not asleep; we are the owners, the proprietors of these natural resources. If we see fit to dispose of them to the United States, it must be at a price and on conditions satisfactory to the private owner or the public of Canada. There is no opportunity given to them to raid our resources- nothing of the kind; and yet the hon. member for North Toronto so argued in this House, and was applauded by every member on the Conservative side. I do not care what President Taft may say in regard to this matter; I do not care what Senator Beveridge may say; and I do not think it is in very good taste for my hon. friend from North Toronto or my good friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) to be guided by what these gentlemen or the'newspapers of the United States have to say on this subject. Let them be guided rather by such papers as the Manchester * Guardian ', which I have quoted. But an effort has been made to bring into this debate all sorts of political entanglements in the United States. There is an effort to found the Conservative opposition to this measure upon the statements of President Taft or of the leader of the Democratic party in the United States Congress or of Senator Beveridge, or of the newspapers of one political creed or another. Surely we as Canadians can judge of this matter irrespective of what the people of the United States may have in their minds.
The statement which has been read here to-day as having been made yesterday in Congress by Mr. Clark has a queer bearing upon another incident which I might mention. Perhaps the greatest annexationist in the United States for many years past has been Speaker Cannon. In a speech which he addressed a few weeks ago to the Grand Army men, and which has been going through the press, he said he was looking forward to the day when Mexico and Canada would be annexed to the United States, and when the American flag would float over the whole of the North American continent, and yet he is the greatest opponent of this measure in the United States Congress to-day. Why should we be upset by any wind of political opinion that blows across the way? The only consideration that should guide us on this question is:	How is this measure as a
pure trade matter going to operate in Canada-will it be to our advantage or against our advantage?
Take another instance of what I consider to be the utter inconsistency of the hon. member for North Toronto on this matter. People sometimes in the heat of debate say things which they do not positively or actually mean; but when a man deliberately sits down and writes an article, copies and recopies it and corrects it, he is taken to mean what he has written. Now, the hon. member for North Toronto has dis-Mr. GUTHRIE.
tinctly said in print, in an elaborate composition in the ' Canadian Magazine ' for the month of December last, entitled, ' Reciprocity-why the United States wants it , by the Rt. Hon. George E. Foster-I suppose that was a Christmas present to the hon. gentleman-this is his own vigorous language:
No sane man will predict any large overflow of natural products from the United States Northward.
And yesterday he argued to a demonstration that market gardeners, fruit growers and pork men would be ruined by the natural products of the United States coming into Canada. I never heard a greater mass of contradiction and inconsistency in the space of a three or four hours' speech during my eleven years experience in the House of Commons.
Now, I am going to take issue with the hon. member for North Toronto on another point, and I think I know a little about this: that is, the question of the price of hogs and cattle as between the United States and Canada. When he made his plea for the pork men, he said that there was a steady supply of pork at a good price in Canada, and that only for a few weeks of the year was the price of pork at Buffalo any higher than in Canada. He makes the same plea with regard to cattle, but I challenge the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), and will let the Toronto ' Mail and Empire ' decide the issue -let him take the columns of that paper during the last five years.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Not its editorials.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
No its market reports, and let him compare Montreal and Toronto markets with Buffalo and Chicago, and he will find that the general average is higher, and markedly so, in Buffalo and Chicago during the last five year period. Now what is it we want? WTe want in my county the privilege of selling our cattle and hogs in Buffalo and other farm produce as well. You say:	What is the use, the Buffalo
market is lower. Well, if it is, are we hurt? We will then sell in the British market, and not touch Buffalo or Chicago. My hon. friend tells us that we have two markets now, the home market and the British; but when this arrangement comes into operation, we shall have three markets, and the one we have not got now, but which we want to get, is by far the largest. We will not send our products to Buffalo or Chicago unless we get better prices than we do at home or in the mother country. Our western people are not going to send any cattle to Chicago unless they can get better prices theTe than elsewhere. If they cannot, they will send them to eastern Canada or Great Britain. What is there unpatriotic or disloyal in that pro-

position? How do business men conduct their business? If the prices in Buffalo are good, they send their wares there; if not they send them elsewhere. Then why should not the government carry on the business of this country on business lines? Why should the government stay its hand at this juncture and deprive our people of one of the great opportunities of their lives?
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) took a rather strange position with regard to the framing of a tariff. He said he did not believe in the way in which our tariff was altered or revised at present. He thought that the system was an improper one. Now the reason I refer to this is that this is a question of vital interest to our people. If my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, desires to place himself on record on this question, I think it well the people should know it. What he said is to be found on pages 3379 and 3380 of ' Hansard.' There he practically proposed that the framing or revision of the tariff should be taken away from this House and placed in the hands of a permanent tariff commission. I do not say, from the language he used, that he gave that as his concluded opinion, but he certainly declared that he thought that was the best method to be adopted. No doubt such a plan would meet the desires of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association; but if my hon. friend would adopt such a system, he would be reversing one of the cardinal principles of the British constitution, which is that the right to tax must remain with the peoples' representatives. The right was established many long years ago, and I have no doubt will survive to the end; but if the leader of the opposition desires to depart from that principle and appoint a permanent tariff commission to regulate our tariff, the sooner the people know it the better. I do not know what his proposal precisely is because he did not put it in very concrete form. He merely said it would be well if we established a permanent tariff commission in Canada, and I take it that means a delegation of the powers of this House to a tariff commission.
If he made any definite statement in regard to the proposed agreement at all, it will be found on page 3374 of ' Hansard.' These are his words:
Now in view of the statistics I have given, are we not moving along the line of material progress and development about as fast as we could expect to go or about as fast as it is desirable to go ?
And in this he was heartily applauded by hon. members opposite. Further on he said:
To use a well known expression, what we have we will hold in that regard. But the
proposals of this government if they mean anything at all, seem to me to mean a considerable departure from that path which we have pursued with so much success.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Would my hon. friend read the whole sentence.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: I thought I had.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman would read further, he will find that it conveys an entirely different impression.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
Well, at all events what the hon. gentleman said will be found on page 3374 of ' Hansard.' The point to which I wished to call special attention is conveyed in these words:
Are we not moving along the line of material progress and development about as fast as we could expect to go or about as fast as it is desriable to go ?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext: Read the lines that follow.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-RECIPROCAL TRADE WITH THE UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
I have no objection. He went on to say:
Are we not at the present time following a perfectly sure and safe path.
Is that the position taken by the leader of the opposition and the Conservative party. Are they reduced to this position: Let us leave well enough alone; we are doing well enough now. Have I not fairly stated the position taken by my ihon, friend, the leader of the opposition. He believes in the good old maxim:	What We
have, we will hold; but let well enough alone. I submit that with regard to trade and commerce that is neither a statesmanlike nor a proper position, nor is it one which the people will endorse. You cannot get a young country like ours, full of vigour, vitality and energy, to sit down and fold its arms and let well enough alone. Is there any period in the business life of any business man when he can conclude to sit down and let well enough alone? He can do this if he retires from business, but we are not retiring from business in Canada. We must keep moving. If we do not go forward, we shall be drifting backward. That is what was the real trouble with the Conservative government from 1890 to 1896. They flattered themselves that they were doing well enough, and were content to stand still, and I am inclined to think that they really believed what they said. I really think that they had convinced themselves of this, and no one was more eloquent on that point than the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). Session after session he pointed to the increase in our exports, which had leaped up some $66,000,000 in eighteen years, to the increase in our bank deposits, to the business disorders in the United States which we have escaped, and urged his audiences to let

well enough alone. But a* a matter of fact we were not progressing at all, but were actually going backwards, and that is what we would do if we were to adopt the policy advocated by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. And I ask any one to note this-and it is the proudest, grandest fact, I think, in connection with the present administration-that from 1896, from the day whereon they took power, you can go to the record of any department, you can open any blue-book we have, and you will see, year by year, during the whole fourteen years, without a single halt in any year, forward-forward-forward ! And the reason for that is that they were not content to say, we are going fast enough; we will let well enough alone, content with the old maxim, ' What we have we'll hold.' That is a good maxim, it is a Liberal maxim; but we add, 'We will get more if possible.' And this is one instance in which we are endeavouring to hold our own and get more.
Now, I must say a word about the effect of the proposal upon what is, perhaps, the largest branch of the subject, so far as Canada is concerned, and that is the export trade of this country. Up to this time I have discussed the effect only on our trade with Great Britain, the effect on our imports from Great Britain and the United States. Now, what about our exports? I believe that, without exaggeration, the exports of Canada to the United States, if. this proposal is adopted, will increase by leaps and bounds. I agree with what has been said by others, and dnferentially stated hy my hon. friend opposite, that the great increase will be in what we may call natural products-I do not mean natural resources; I mean the products of the farm chiefly. I note that we only sold to the United States last year $113,000,000 worth of goods, but I note, also, that we bought from them $223,000,000 worth. And that, according to my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster)-and I will not say it is my opinion-constitutes an adverse balance of trade, which, in the end, has to be met through the banks with cash. My hon. friend from North Toronto has had an annual complaint against this government, an annual criticism of its policy. Whereas trade conditions with the United Kingdom weTe satisfactory-we sold them more than we purchased from them, the balance of trade, he said, was in favour of Canada- he argued, and pages in ' Hansard ' will show the argument, that our trade with the United States has been absolutely unsatisfactory; in fact, he said the condition of things had become startling, that we were only selling them a small quantity as compared with the goods which we were purchasing from them, and ultimately this balance would have to he settled. He discussed it as an adverse balance of trade, Mr. GUTHRIE.
and, from his point of view, I must say, he discussed it very ably. It is a vexed question, it is about as intricate and difficult a problem as any that I know of, and I do not feel able to cope with the argument of my hon. friend in regard to the adverse balance of trade. But I think the present proposal should cause a genial smile, ' the smile that won't come off,' to illumine his countenance, because he must see, if his statement in the House is correct, that the balance of trade as between Canada and the United States will now shortly be in favour of Canada. Speaking in this House, in March, 1908, the hon. gentleman gave a statement of the goods exported and imported as between Canada and the United States, which statement appears at page 5273 of ' Hansard ' of that year, and shows:
Ten years Conservative rule, adverse balance of trade of $167,841,393.
Ten years of Liberal rule, an adverse balance of trade of $384,950,596.
Then he proceeds:
In 12 months ending June 30. 1907, the imports from United States were $206,715,914, the exports to the United States, $82,194,661, and the adverse balance of trade reached the enormous sum of $124,521,253.
Now I think that is a somewhat startling showing. This adverse balance of trade has to be met, it has to be met every month, every three months, every year. You cannot run credit for that adverse balance of trade, it has to be adjusted through the banks and through the business of the country. Now let me point out that in this statement I have simply taken the exports of home products, because I wanted to show the exact relation of trade as regards the export of Canada's own produce, to the foreign produce we were importing. Now if you deduct the foreign produce also exported to the United States in that period of ten years, it amounts to $30,000,000. Subtracting that, taking both the home and foreign products, the adverse balance of trade against us in those ten years, with the United States, was $552,000,000.
That would be an average of $52,000,000 a year of an adverse balance. Turning to page 5277, we find the hon. gentleman saying:
Now, what I think about the balance of trade is this: That the balance of trade in the 6rst place must be settled presently. It is not as if I could go to my friend here and borrow $100 from him and give him a note for three years and pay him interest. These international balances are not arranged in that way. They have to be adjusted every month, every three months, every six months at the longest and they are so adjusted, and the banks are the mechanism which we use for that adjustment. That is the first point I make. We have got to pay our balances: we cannot run credit from year to year on them. Now, they can only be paid either in goods or in gold, and whichever it is it is our export trade which in the final analy-

sis has to pay our bills and we have nothing else to pay them with. Well, so far as trade and navigation figures go you may call that a trade balance if you like. That is the visible trade of the country. You might so far as that goes balance one by the other, or be in debt, or have a profit. But it may be said: That is not all that is coming and going between the countries; there are invisible exports and imports. And that is true. But yet it is absolutely true that in the end even the actual international balance has got to be settled by exports from the country that owes and it can be paid in no other way.
There is hope, and I think a splendid hope, that the result of the present proposal, if carried into effect, will be to adjust that adverse balance of trade. There is no doubt, in the opinion of my hon. friend from North Toronto, in the opinion of any member of this House, I think, that Canada, under this arrangement, is going to sell a tremendous quantity of goods to the United States, a tremendous quantity of our natural products. And if I may take the written statement of my hon. friend from North Toronto upon the question: * No sane man will predict any large overflow of natural products from the United States northward.' The balance will be in our favour. And I add to that, we need not fear an increase of imnorts of American manufactured goods; there is nothing to warrant the idea that we will have more than we have now. The reductions in the tariff on these goods have been so small that there is no encouragement for more importations, and gradually our manufacturing establishments are assuming-larger and larger proportions, and are able to produce more and more goods and at lower prices, so that with the reasonable tariff which is still retained under schedules ' B ' and ' D,' there is not the slightest reason for believing that there will be any increase in United States manufactured goods coming into Canada, Trade will go from the north southward. I, in my county, look to a heavy increase in the exportation of cattle, sheep, lambs, poultry and the like. In my county, and in the counties surrounding, we looked to the old barley crop, which, prior to the McKinley tariff of 1901, was a vastly paying crop in the province of Ontario. Barley, which used to bring 85 cents a bushel, latterly brought [DOT]only 55 cents. Barley, I believe, this week in Toronto brings 60 cents, and in Buffalo 90 cents. Barley, no doubt, will be a large and profitable crop in the province of Ontario if this proposed arrangement should take effect.
I cannot say so much in regard to wheat. The wheat that is grown in my county is largely used for local milling purposes, and for the purpose of feeding stock. I am not familiar with the movement of wheat as between Canada and the United States, so I prefer to leave that question
to ,be settled by those who are familiar with it. I do say this, however, that so far as I have .been able to examine the matter-.and I have looked into it with some care-I cannot see any reason why we should expect any very great increase in the price of wheat for exportation to the United States. There may be ta reason, and there may be an increased price, but I am not able exactly to find out how it will come about. I do think, however, that the time is coming, the time indeed is almost at hand, when the United States will not be exporting wheat. The time is coming, indeed the time I believe is at hand, when tlie United States will not export cattle. By the end of the present year, it is said, there will be no exported oattle from the United States ; and if the figures I have seen are correct, the time is .almost at hand when there will be no wheat exported from the United States. I think there is a great chance of the wheat growers of the west obtaining in the markets of the United States an advantage which penha-ps they do not enjoy now, as the price of wheat is still regulated in the British market. I have taken trouble to look up some facts in regard to wheat, chiefly having reference to a statement made in the address of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition.

That is in regard to a tariff commission ; I said all I intended to say on that. I was discussing -the question, of wheat, and chiefly in reference to a remark made by the leader of the opposition in the course of his speech to the effect that if Canadians were not particular we would find that foreign countries like the Argentine Republic would send their products to Great Britain, and I was under the impression that they send a large quantity of their natural products there now. Great Britain is not disposed to he over particular as to where she purchases those products, and there is no benefit to her to buv from Canada rather than in Argentina. So I looked up the reports, and I found in the library a volume published annually known as the '-Statesman's YearBook ' for 1910. And here I wish to remark, that in looking through the volume I saw that some vandal has cut out 15 or 20 pages of the -most valuable information in it. I mention this, for one reason because I have -noticed the same thing in regard to other statistical works. It ought to he brought to the attention of those having care of the library, that mutilation-" of this kind should not be allowed, an! that anybody who does mutilate -a volume should -be deprived of the privileges of the library. However, I found the report that I required, and I find in the ' Statesman's Year-Book ' for 1910, that wheat imported into Great Britain during 1909 from all parts of the British Empire amounted to 69,000,000 bushels. The figures given in the volume are given in hundred weights, 60 pounds to the bushel -and 100 pounds to the 100 weight. I find that the total imports of wheat into Great Britain for 1909 were 163,000,000 bushels. I thought it rather strange to see a published interview with the Hon. Robert Rogers within the last three or four days, I think after he left Ottawa, in a Minneapolis newspaper, in which he expressed himself as opposed to the present trade arrangement, and said that if this arrangement were negatived, in a very Mr. LENNOX.
short time, I think he said next year, Canada would be exporting to Great Britain
200.000.	000 bushels of wheat. I think, on the face of it, that statement is ridiculous, because all that Great Britain takes from the whole world is 163,000,000 bushels. It is interesting to know where she gets her wheat. Have we interfered with Argentina in that respect? Why, Great Britain takes more wheat from the Argentine Republic than from any other quarter of the globe. From the Argentine Republic in 1909 she took 33,000,000 bushels ; from Russia, poor distressed, protected Russia, 30,000,000 bushels ; from Canada, 27,500,000 ; from the United States, 24,000,000 ; from India,
24.000.	000, and the balance is made up of wheat- from Chili, Australia, Lower Egypt, and all other quarters of the world. I wont -give the statistics in regard to flour, though the member for North Toronto did give them, and probably they are correct. Now, what is the -position with regard to wheat in the United States? I looked up the statistical year-book of the United States for 1910, and here let me say that the statistical information -prepared by the United States government is far in advance of that prepared in Canada ; it is in a more convenient form. I have the greatest difficulty in finding the information I require in our -blue-nooks, and I think it would be a good thing if our government sent a deputation to Washington for the purpose of learning a -better method of preparing statistics.
However, in the United States Statistical Year-book, I find that the greatest year of production was 1892, when they produced
748.000.	000 bushels. The exportation that year was 235,000,000 bushels to all places in the world. That is nine years before the next item that I give. The wheat produced in 1909 was 664,000,000 bushels, there was consumed in the United States 550,000,000 bushels, and there was exported
114.000.	000 bushels. But, take the year 1908, and you will find that in that year they exported 163,000,000 bushels-not 114,-000,000-and that they consumed only 490,000,000 bushels, whereas the following year they consumed 550,000,000 bushels, and so the ratio of consumption is increasing, while exportation is decreasing. It has been said by such men as Jas. J. Hill, in fact, I think the President of the United States-anyway by competent authority- that- it is only a question of time when the exportation of wheat from the United States will stop. Then, I take the question of cattle. My statement with -regard to cattle is hardly as precise. In some cases numbers are given and in some cases values are given. I find that in England, in 1909, there was received from all sources 321,000 head of cattle; no value given. In the United States Statistical Year-book for 1910 I find that in 1900 the United States ex*

ported 397,000 head of cattle, and that in 1909 they exported only 207,000 head, a decrease of almost 45 per cent. The value of cattle exported in 1900 was $30,000,000, and in 1909 $18,000,000. But I have it from pretty fair authority that during the present year-that is 1911-there will be no cattle exported from the United States.

speechtext:
No, I have only taken into account the export of live cattle. I also have this to say with regard to the cattle trade and the export of cattle finished in my county, that during last fall and summer fine export steers weighing 1,400 pounds were shipped to Toronto for export to Liverpool, but on account of the better price being paid in Chicago they were reshipped from Toronto back to Chicago. This has not been in a single case, but in many cases, and, as my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture reminds me, they were shipped to Chicago in spite of the duty. I believe that in all western Ontario we will ship a tremendous amount of live stock to the United States if this proposal succeeds. It will be more convenient to ship to Buffalo than to Liverpool. The freight rates will be less, and I believe that on the average the price will be higher-I do not say to any great extent higher-'but on ia 1,400 pound beast, if only one cent a pound, that is $14 to -the farmer, and that, is a most, important increase in price to him. I believeTHat the price of mutton and lamb is higher in Buffalo on the average than in Toronto, and Buffalo is the market for lambs for the southwestern portion of Ontario. They now pay a duty of 75 cents on lambs, and of $1.50 on sheep. I believe the farmer will get a better price and have a better market for sheep and lambs if this tariff change takes place. Turnips we ship in large quantities. Turnips are a paying crop in our countv, because we feed and ship a great quantity of them. The regulations which the United States have been enforcing at the border have interfered with a profitable trade in that product. Turnips now pay a duty of 25 per cent or something of the kind, .but it is not only the rate of duty but also the regulations o:f which we complain. A turnip shipper told me that turnips which ihe has bought for 10 and 12 cents a bushel are revalued at the border at as high as 18 and 20 cents, and that he has lost on the transaction because of such re-valuation. The United States have some system by which they regulate what they believe to be the actual value of any article. These drawbacks to trade, I understand, aie to be removed, or it is the intention of both parties that they will
be removed. Potatoes, which, likewise, are very largely produced in my county, and in counties similarly situated, are placed on the free list. VVe will ship a tremendous quantity of such articles, and of poultry, butter and barley large quantifies will be shipped to the United States, which we do net ship there now.
I mention these facts to show that the balance of trade is going from the north to the south, and that there will not be a great quantity of trade coming from the south to the north if this arrangement is carried out as it stands before the House to-day. I do not know sufficient about the case of the fruit growers to discuss it intelligently. But I hear on the one hand the cry that if this trade arrangement goes into force the cost of living will 'be increased. and I hear, on the other hand, the cry that the cost of fruit to the grower will be lowered, the cost of vegetables to the grower will be lowered, and that the price of meat and bacon and beef products will be lowered-so the packers' association tell the people of Canada. I will give my own best judgment in regard to that question. I am as convinced as I can be of anything that the great farming community of this country, representing sixty per cent of our population, is going to be very materially benefited. The farmers are going to make money, they are going to make a lot of money, and year after year they will make more money as long as this arrangement lasts.
What about- the people who live in the villages, towns and cities? It would be illogical to declare that there would be an increase in the price of farming commodities and no increase in the price of living. What I sav with regard to that is that there is not going to be anything like any immediate jump, there is going to be a fair increase in value, and there will be a steady value, there will ibe no fluctuation between this country and that country, as there will toe no tariff between them. There will be a fair increase of value, and where you have a general prosperity and increased receipts by the great bulk of the people of this country, it will be in the nature of a national prosperity, and every man, woman and child in the land must feel the result of it. I believe that it will be a tremendous advantage to the people of the northwest, the people of the prairie provinces, if this trade arrangement is put in force. It will increase the rapidity with which that great country is being settled up. What would be the effect on the manufacturing industries of Ontario if we had one million more farmers in the northwest raising wheat and cattle? That is the true policy of the east and west, and I wish to be understood as not to say one single word against the development of our own manufacturing industries.

One reason I have for appreciating this trade arrangement in particular is that our commissioners, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs, have scrupulously avoided anything in that arrangement which could be an injury to any section of our manufacturing industries in the Dominion of Canada as far as I am aware. I wish to see them enjoy a fair amount of protection. I am not an out-and-out free trader; in fact, I disagiee with the principles of free trade as expressed in this House unless we have the broad world to trade freely with. I believe W'e must have some kind of protection in Ontario.

Well, that is a subject I am not competent to discuss. I do not know that I had better venture upon that subject because I do not know anything about it. I am talking about conditions as I find them. I have no quarrel with any industry because I believe that if we adopt a measure that will promote the general prosperity you help the manufacturing and every other interest in Canada. I am not supported very largely by the proprietors of factories in Guelph. I am sorry I am not, I have tried to support them, tout the fact is I am not. In Guelph we have a very large industry manufacturing all grades of hardware. We have another large factory manufacturing sewing machines and cream separators. We have a carpet factory making Brussels and other high grade carpets. We have a large pipe industry making iron pipe and employing 200 or 300 men. We have the Bell Organ and Piano Company, we have an axle works, two stove foundries and many other important manufacturing concerns. I am sorry they do not yield me much support at election time, and I think they should. However, I want to support them if I can and so long as our tariff, kept down to a revenue basis, affords enough protection to protect them I am satisfied with that feature of the tariff. I am not a high protectionist; I think high protection in Canada would be a ridiculous proposal, hut for the last five or ten years Guelph's shipments Mr. GUTHRIE.
have gone where? To the Northwest. Where have they gone from Toronto and other cities in Ontario and Quebec? They are finding their best market in the Northwest to-day. Give them a million more prosperous farmers out there with a convenient market, increase their purchasing power, and you will increase their demands and then if you maintain a revenue tariff with sufficient incidental protection you will increase the industry in every manufacturing establishment in Canada. You will increase the price of wages, you will increase the demand for labour. Make the great bulk of the people of this country prosperous on their farms and the cry of ' back to the land,' will have some effect, and a large number of people who are today coming into the towns and cities who are not mechanics or artisans will go back to the land where they can make a reasonable profit for their labour. You create a demand in that way in the labour market.
I believe in a thorough examination of the
immigration that is coming into Canada._I
congratulate my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior and the branch of his department that has charge of immigration jn the efficiency of that service at present. We have a better class of people coming in, more suited to conditions in this country. We have a carefully selected immigration coming in, and I believe that the figures this year will run to about one half million people, nearly all for the ^Northwest. Place these on the farms, make them comfortable, and increase their purchasing power and you solve the problem of the cost of living. Give an artisan in my city an opportunity of earning $2 or $2.50 more per week, and he is more than repaid for any extra cost of living that may be engendered by the farmer receiving more for his produce. In the ease of the individual, the proportion of increase is very small. An additional fourteen dollars on a beast to the farmer means but one or two cents extra on a piece of steak to the customer in the city. Let the clerk have a chance to get a better salary. On what does the ordinary merchant in a country or village store depend? On the prosperity of the surrounding farmers. We have it in Guelph, they have it in other towns the same way, our great commerce is between the townships and the city, between the villages and the city. Give these farmers more money to spend, and the merchants in town will make more. They can pay more salaries to tiheir clerks if the farmers of the country enjoy a greater power of purchasing. They wdll want more home made goods and more British goods, and it is on that principle I argue that the purchasing power will be increased and imports from Great Britain will be increased and not decreased-and the preference will be a real preference.

I take no stock whatever in the cry that we are going t-o ruin the Taiilroads; the railroads have always been able to take care of themselves. I take no stock in the cry that we will frighten British capital. I believe the hon. member from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) yesterday based 75 per cent of his argument on the declaration or letter written by Mr. Blake in 1891 upon a proposal radically different from the one now before this House. That was a policy of unrestricted reciprocity or commercial union; this is a proposal for <a very limited trade agreement. The one was to be in the shape of a definite binding treaty, this is in the shape of a treaty which we or the United States can set aside at will, which will remain in force only so long as it proves mutually beneficial. The arguments of Mr. Blake, for whom I have the highest respect, do not pertain to the question now under consideration in this committee, although they might have pertained and probably did pertain, to the question under discussion at the time Mr. Blake wrote his letter. But what about the railroads? Who says the railways of Canada have any fear of this? Who has the right to say so? Who has heard from them in regard to the subject? Have any railroads pronounced upon the question? The only railroad man who has pronounced upon it is Sir Donald Mann of the Canadian Northern. It was rumored in one paper that Sir William Mackenzie had said something but this was promptly denied by Sir William. But Sir Donald Mann is quite clear in his statement^ which Js_ published in a very respectable financial paper in Canada called the ' Financial Post ' in the issue of February 4. Sir Donald Mann there says:
The products of the farm, of the sea and of the mine are entitled to especial consideration. Nor should the lumbermen be overlooked. Timber is a crop which ripens, and should be reaped. If it is not, it deteriorates. He who cuts down one ripe tree and plants one or more in its place is a producer of wealth.
If we have seven or eight millions of people in Canada, with a free market for the producer, and to that number we add the 95 millions of the United States, we are assisting the most important industries in Canada.
Next in importance to the producer comes the manufacturer and it is the duty of the government to provide increased market facilities for both. The United States has ceased to export cattle, and may soon cease to export wheat. The balance between production and consumption is drawing nearer adjustment. If ^ it were possible to prevent grain from going south, without injury to the producer,
I would say avoid a treaty or other reciprocal arrangement, but it is beyond our power to hold our wheat within British territory. The United States can remove the tariff whenever it suits her convenience so to do, without consulting us.
With regard to the export of wheat, Canada
will have her own lines of railway across the continent as well as ships upon the 6ea. This will enable them to take grain for export from the producer to the consumer, without any division of rates, and, in the same way, manufactured goods as return cargoes from the producer to the consumer in the west. On the other hand, going south through the United States, wheat for export would have to pass over three or four lines of railways, and thence by independent vessels to European markets. This through rate, which is necessarily low, would be divided among three or four transportation companies, making it impossible to compete with Canadian through lines. Depend upon it Canadian ralways handling natural products of the west for export will retain the traffic on their own tracks and in their own vessels to destination.
Personally I would prefer to have a preference between the United Kingdom and the Dominion, and between the Dominion and other colonies. This preference should be increased from time to time until, say in 25 years, the cost of production would reach a common point throughout the empire. Then we would be able to have free trade within the empire, and protection against the nonBritish nations.
That is a very strong statement and it is the only authoritative announcement by any important railroad man I have seen. Why then raise that cry about railroads? The railroads are not afraid of it. What are the Canadian Pacific railway doing. They have completed their lines to Chicago and Duluth, owning now the Wisconsin Central through the United States and the Sault line to Duluth. What are the Canadian Northern doing? At this moment They are completing their line from Winnipeg to Duluth and by the first of August that line will be in operation and it will be carrying grain in September. The railroads are not afraid of it. Who is afraid of it? I do not know that the Manufacturers^ Association have made any pronouncement upon the subject. I do not think they have. They probably will oppose it on the ground that they have opposed almost everything that emanates from this government in regard to tariffs.
Then, what is their real objection ? I think the weakest objection I have heard, and one which it is almost useless to discuss, is that a good trade agreement between Canada and the United States, which will be beneficial to this country- and if it is not, , we will abrogate it-and which will be beneficial to the United States-and if it is not, they will abrogate it-will lead in some way to a commercial or political union between the two countries. Some people say-I do not think they are very brave in the idea-that it is the entering of the wedge, that it is the beginning of the end. Well, I cannot see ;n a trade measure anything of the kind. There is nothing to support such an idea There has been no experience, so far as I

March, 1849. Lord Elgin said:
There has been a vast deal of talk about annexation, as is unfortunately always the case when there is anything to agitate the public mind. A great deal of this talk is, however, bravado, and a great deal the mere product of thoughtlessness. Undoubtedly it is in some quarters the utterances of very serious conviction; and if England will not make the sacrifices which are absolutely necessary to put the colonists here in as good a position commercially as the citizens of the States-in order to which free navigation and reciprocal trade with the States are indispensable-if not only the organs of the league, but those of the government and of the Peel party, are always writing as if it were an admitted fact that colonies, and more especially Canada, are a burden, to be endured only because they cannot be got rid of, the end may lie nearer than we wot of.
In November of the same year Lord Elgin wrote to Lord Grey:
But if things remain at their present footing in this respect, there is nothing before us Mr. GUTHRIE.
but violent agitation, ending in convulsion or annexation. And I much fear that no measure but the establishment of reciprocal trade between Canada and the States, or the imposition of a duty on the produce of the States when imported into England, will remove it.
Now, that was the cause of the disturbance at that time.

The hour of adjournment is so near, that I cannot continue this discussion longer. I have heard no substantial reason advanced against this proposal, which will bear investigation. Every interest of Canada, is guarded. It gives us three markets, instead of two. Every interest of Great Britain is guarded. If a day comes when Great Britain is able to enter into better arrangements with the colonies and to bring us all together, our hands are free. If we become a greater and more prosperous people, if we become a richer people, we shall be all the stronger as a British nation and a part of the British Empire, and we shall never, with my consent, be other than a part of the British Empire. But why mix this matter up with questions affecting our political relations? The whole and sole question foT us is, have we made a good bargain? As for me and the part of the country which I represent, this proposal will be welcomed as one of the most progressive acts of a government which for 14 years has shown nothing but progress, development and success in Canada.
Progress reported.
